The rocks west of the Methow River and east of the Smith Canyon fault were originally mapped as Leecher Metamorphics by Barksdale (1975), who considered the mylonitized and phyllonitized greenschist-facies rocks to be products of shearing and retrograde metamorphism of Leecher Metamorphic rocks. Although these rocks may have been formed from the Leecher Metamorphics, they are distinctly different in metamorphic and structural characters and have been assigned here to the McClure Mountain unit. Skarn zones in marble, formed at the contact of the Leecher Metamorphics with the Texas Creek stock, contain scheelite, chalcopyrite, molybdenite, pyrite, magnetite, and hematite in a gangue of calcite, epidote, and garnet. Heterogeneous metamorphic rocks of the Leecher also serve as host to a gold deposit at the Minnie mine. The Leecher Metamorphics may be correlative with the Salmon Creek Schists and Gneisses, but the Leecher Metamorphics do not contain abundant marble and sillimanite-bearing schists that are present in the Salmon Creek unit. Near the contact with the Summit-Frazer trondhjemitic gneiss, the Leecher Metamorphics are migmatitic and are intruded by the Summit-Frazer trondhjemitic gneiss. The age of the Leecher unit is not known. It is assigned an age of pre-Cretaceous because it is intruded by the Cretaceous Texas Creek stock and the Cretaceous-Jurassic Okanogan complex (Summit-Frazer gneiss). Field relations of the Leecher to the Methow Gneiss suggest that the latter intruded the Leecher and together they were ductilely deformed before intrusion of the Okanogan complex. This relation allows the possibility that the Leecher is considerably older than Cretaceous. The Leecher may be equivalent to the amphibolite, schist, and gneiss of Alta Lake and to the amphibolite and schist of Twentyfive Mile Creek, which, by extension to the younger gneissic rocks of the Holden, Twisp and Chelan areas, may be Permian. This correlation with the Leecher is highly speculative.

"Core and western margin of Tatoosh pluton of Mount Rainier National Park; pinkish to light brownish-gray medium-grained equigranular hornblende-biotite granodiorite; dated at 17.5 m.y.B.P. (U-Pb, zircon; Mattinson, 1977) and 14.7 m.y.B.P. (K-Ar, biotite; Fiske and others, 1963"; Hammond, 1980; Wright, 1960); a coarse-grained amphibole-pyroxene quartz diorite representing the quartz-diorite phase of the Nisqually granodiorite.

Brown to red oxidized basaltic breccia and tuff with thin basalt flows. Crudely bedded. Dense black microporphyritic olivine basalt; microphenocrysts of plagioclase, clinopyroxene, and olivine in intersertal groundmass of plagioclase, clinopyroxene, opaque minerals, and brown glass. Weathers red and is locally columnar jointed. Locally altered to siliceous white rock.

Basaltic andesite, basalt, and rhyolite in flows, breccia, and tuff interbedded with tuffaceous to feldspathic sandstone, conglomerate, and minor argillite. Basalt in the upper part of the section forms dark brown columnar flows. Basaltic andesite generally dark-green to gray, massive, aphyric, and dense. Light-green to white rhyolite, found as thick flows, typically weathering light-green to white with flow laminations; commonly spherulitic. Rocks are mostly highly altered to a dense mat of chlorite, epidote, calcite, and sericite; porphyritic and trachytoid textures are relict. Most bedding in volcanic members is obscure except in some water-laid tuffs. Many rocks recrystallized by thermal metamorphism near Tertiary plutons, reaching pyroxene-hornfels facies adjacent to unfaulted contacts with plutons.  South of Skykomish, rocks of Barlow Pass(?) Volcanics are mostly heterogeneous, light-tan to dark-gray-green, rhyolitic to andesitic breccia and feldspar porphyry. Rocks identified as andesite in the field generally contain at least trace amounts of quartz in thin section. Crystal-rich andesite and dacite breccia contains andesite, dacite, and rhyolite clasts, sandstone, metasedimentary rocks, chert, siltstone quartz, foliated polycrystalline quartz, potassium feldspar, and plagioclase. Crystal-rich greenish rhyodacite breccia has platy cleavage. Amygdaloidal andesite(?) and andesite(?) porphyry, in part having crude columns, are also present. Plagioclase is commonly altered to calcite and chlorite. Pyrite is locally present. Includes probable intrusive rhyolite porphyry on Money Creek. Many volcanic rocks in the Barlow Pass(?) Volcanics are partly to strongly recrystallized by nearby Tertiary plutons.

East-west elongate, undeformed, biotite quartz monzonite, granite, and monzogranite. Light-gray, fine- to medium-grained (0.25-1.0 mm), with nearly equal proportions of interlocking quartz and white anhedral orthoclase. Biotite constitutes less than 1 percent of the rock. Leucoxene is present as an alteration product of rare garnets. Alaskite is present in two masses less than 80 m long and transects all other parts of the pluton. The pluton is thought to be a magmatic differentiate with two phases: a central porphyritic biotite granite, and a nonporphyritic biotite quartz monzonite border phase. A small late-phase alaskitic body is also present. This rock, at the eastern margin of the pluton, is Precambrian amphibolite intruded and partially assimilated by the porphyritic monzogranite. The pluton is intruded by lamprophyre dikes, mineralized quartz veins, aplite, and pegmatite dikes. The pluton has sharp intrusive contacts with border rocks. Contact metamorphism has affected all metasedimentary and metavolcanic rocks along its border. The inner metamorphic aureole of the Spirit pluton was assigned to the hornblende-hornfels facies. Carbonate rocks of the Metaline Formation 3 m or closer to the pluton contain an assemblage of diopside, calcite, wollastonite +/- idocrase +/- forsterite(?) +/- garnet; at distances of more than 3 m and less than 100 m, a common assemblage in the Metaline is tremolite, diopside, and quartz. At distances of 100 m to 600 m from the border of the pluton the assemblage of tremolite, calcite, and quartz is common in these carbonate rocks. Pelitic Precambrian rocks on Huckleberry Mountain 3 m or closer to the border of the pluton contain an assemblage of quartz, biotite, muscovite +/- cordierite +/- andalusite. Biotite from the nonporphyritic border phase at the west end of the pluton gave a K-Ar age of 102 +/- 2.8 Ma. Hornblende from the quartz diorite gave an age of 96.3 +/- 3.0 Ma. Nearly west-trending structures probably controlled the emplacement of the pluton; the pluton clearly crosscuts folding.

On Money Creek, hypersthene-clinopyroxene gabbro, medium-grained, subophitic to locally uralitic. Commonly layered containing well-aligned calcic plagioclase. On Palmer Mountain, medium-grained uralitic gabbro and quartz gabbro composed of tightly packed calcic plagioclase with uralite patches and uralite pseudomorphous after subophitic pyroxene(?). On Middle Fork of Snoqualmie River, heterogeneous, uralitized pyroxene gabbro to mafic biotite-hornblende tonalite; strongly thermally metamorphosed.
Biotite granite and granodiorite, commonly with large twinned perthite crystals. Minor hornblende. Color Index=4-17.

Volcanic breccia and conglomerate, pyroclastic flows, and indurated mud flows that outcrop west of Colville. The breccia is composed of 95 percent rounded to subangular clasts of gray porphyritic augite dacite flow rock, which is texturally and petrographically similar to dacite stratigraphically below it. The matrix is tuffaceous at some localities. Fragments range from less than 2 cm to 2 m in diameter, but average about 4 cm; beds range from 10 cm to more than 100 m in thickness. Large boulders are more common near the base of the unit; the breccia is well sorted near Gold Creek. This unit is approximately 274 to 305 m thick. May have been deposited as lahars and pyroclastic breccia.

Includes 45-m-thick, crudely bedded deposit of reddish scoria and bombs capped by thin flow of light-gray olivine basalt on crest of Bethel Ridge; deposit occupies a channel eroded in Miocene-Oligocene tuffaceous rocks unit; remnant basalt flow found at west end of Bethel Ridge; also includes a poorly exposed, light-gray olivine basalt flow or plug on Russell Ridge 1.5 km southeast of Ironstone Mountain; most likely late Miocene or Pliocene because it rests on Bethel Ridge which was probably once covered by Grande Ronde basalt (middle Miocene).

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Windy Hill, quartz dioritic orthogneiss of
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Quartz diorite gneiss that is mineralogically similar to the Reed Creek quartz dioritic gneiss, but is distinguished from the Reed Creek by its higher color index and lower quartz to plagioclase ratio. The Windy Hill quartz dioritic orthogneiss is equivalent in part to the "metagranitoid rocks" of Rinehart (1981), which vary from quartz dioritic to quartz monzonitic in composition. The Windy Hill unit crops out on the slopes of Windy Hill east of Buzzard Lake (T. 34 N., R. 25 E.). It intrudes the Salmon Creek Schists and Gneisses and is intruded by the Conconully granodiorite. Intrusive contact relations with the Salmon Creek Schists and Gneisses, and relict plagioclase zoning indicate that the Windy Hill quartz dioritic orthogneiss is a metamorphosed pluton.

Streaky, swirled and irregular light- and dark-colored biotite-hornblende tonalite gneiss including and grading into hornblende schist, hornblende-biotite schist, mafic amphibolite, hornblende- diorite pegmatite, and hornblendite. Highly variable in composition and texture. Heteroblastic to xenomorphic granular with unzoned andesine and green hornblende. Anastomosing dikes of fine-grained to pegmatitic-hornblende tonalite, diorite, and gabbro.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: mostly Vashon Stade in western WA; unnamed in eastern WA
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Outwash sand, pebble to cobble gravel, and lacustrine clay, silt, and sand deposited during glacial advance by proglacial streams and in proglacial lakes. Typically light gray to light brown. Sands are commonly thick, poorly to well-sorted, well-bedded, and fine-grained, with lenses of coarser sand and gravel. Locally contains nonglacial sediments; generally firm, unoxidized, overlain by till.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Old Snowy Mountain, feeders for flows of
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Light-gray, phyric hypersthene andesite; very fine grained dense andesite; forms lava flows in the upper Lake Creek (southeast of Packwood Lake) and in the Cispus River valley to the south of the Mount Rainier area; erupted from vents near the top of Old Snowy Mountain; this vent area was also center of the Plio-Pleistocene Goat Rocks stratovolcano; may be related to Tieton Andesite, which erupted about 1 m.y.B.P. (K-Ar age date) from vents just east of the Old Snowy vents.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: western melange belt, argillite and graywacke of the
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Pervasively sheared, scaly matrix of mostly argillite containing steep-sided, outcrop- to mountain-sized phacoids of purplish, reddish, gray, and black, fine- to coarse-grained and pebbly, lithofeldspathic, volcanolithic, and subquartzose sandstone interbedded with black argillite. Well-bedded marine sandstone and argillite and subordinate pervasively sheared argillite. Purplish, reddish, gray and black, fine- to coarse-grained and pebbly lithofeldspathic and volcanolithic subquartzose sandstone interbedded with black argillite. Sandstone commonly is mixed type containing clasts of mostly plagioclase, chert, volcanic rocks, and quartz, as well as sandstone, siltstone, phyllite, biotite, muscovite, and epidote. Where more strongly deformed, unstable grains are broken down into anastomosing shear zones or smeared out into indistinct chloritic matrix. Alteration minerals include calcite, chlorite, sericite, limonite, epidote, and prehnite. Near Tertiary plutons, rocks are hornfelsic, commonly show conspicuous metamorphic biotite. Sedimentary features such as graded bedding and load casts are locally well preserved. Contains highly folded, sheared and recrystallized banded cherts. Unit includes metagabbro, both polymictic and quartz-pebble conglomerate, limestone, metavolcanic rocks, metatonalite, and shale-chip breccia. East of North Bend, sandstone and argillite are highly sheared, forming outcrops of lenticular sandstone clasts in crudely foliated argillite. This deformational style is typical of western melange belt in exposures. Locally cut by greenstone (metadiabase) dikes.

Pink orthoclase and chalky white plagioclase (oligoclase-andesine) phenocrysts as much as 10 mm long and biotite phenocrysts less than 2 mm long, in an aphanitic holocrystalline groundmass of orthoclase and quartz. Mafic clots of hornblende and augite are found locally. Feldspars are commonly sericitized, and mafic minerals are generally altered to chlorite, calcite, and sphene. These intrusions crop out in the Toroda Creek graben, in the northern part of the Republic graben, and at First Thought Mountain near Orient. The porphyritic trachyte plugs and dikes cut the Sanpoil Volcanics, Herron Creek suite intrusions, and Eocene porphyritic dacite plugs.  Abundant plugs and dikes of porphyritic trachyte, dacite, and andesite in the Republic graben and in part of the northern segment of the Toroda Creek graben. Smaller intrusions and dikes are found near Kettle Falls, and on Kelly Hill. Whole-rock, major-element geochemical data indicate that these intrusions are dacitic, andesitic, trachyandesitic, and trachytic in composition. The intrusions are compositionally similar to flows in the Sanpoil Volcanics, suggesting that they are hypabyssal intrusive equivalents of the flows. Northeast of Beebe trachyte porphyry dikes that contain 0.5-cm K-feldspar phenocrysts in a fine-grained groundmass can be found. Mafic minerals are altered and unrecognizable; green epidote is present.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Loop Creek pluton, granodiorite of Hall Mountain
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: A small, poorly exposed body that extends across the Pend Oreille River to the base of Ruby Mountain. It contains sparse muscovite and locally is coarser than most Hall Mountain-type rock. The coarser grained parts resemble the Reeder Creek pluton on the west side of Priest Lake in Idaho. In thin section, medium- to coarse-grained felsic minerals are surrounded by thin rims of very fine-grained feldspar, quartz, and mica, suggesting the rock may have been quenched. The border zone at the base of Ruby Mountain is fine-grained. Quartz veins are ubiquitous and locally abundant. Pyrite is common in much of this pluton, even where no alteration is apparent. Chiefly leucocratic, muscovite-biotite granodiorite, but ranges from tonalite to calcic monzogranite. Muscovite in the granodiorite of Hall Mountain is spatially associated with biotite and appears to be primary, although it postdates the biotite. Biotite is generally brown or olive green. K-feldspar is microcline that contains inclusions of fairly large plagioclase and, less commonly, biotite crystals. Accessory minerals include epidote, clinozoisite, allanite, zircon, apatite, rutile, and minor opaque minerals. This group of distinct plutons, which has narrow contact metamorphic aureoles and chilled margins of finer-grained rock, is generally thought to be higher-level plutons. They are genetically related to the granodiorite of Reeder Creek.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Napeequa unit, Chelan Mountains terrane, Rainbow Lake Schist
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Biotite schist and quartzite (metachert), less common amphibolite, marble, and calc-silicate, and rare metaperidotite. The most distinctive rock type is a staurolite-garnet-biotite schist. Sillimanite-bearing staurolite schist occurs locally near Rainbow Lake. Leucocratic sills and pegmatites intrude the schist; some of them have been folded with the schists. Tight folds of foliation are common. An axial-planar foliation is well developed, and a mineral lineation commonly parallels fold axes. Schist, gneiss, amphibolite, meta-gabbro, and ultramafite. This oceanic unit of the Chelan Mountains terrane includes the Rainbow Lake Schist, Twisp Valley Schist, and rocks of the Napeequa River area. The rocks of the Napeequa River area have been subdivided, whereas the Rainbow Lake Schist  and Twisp Valley Schist remain largely undivided.  The age of the Napeequa unit is problematic due to the paucity of datable materials. Recent discordant Rb-Sr data from the rocks of the Napeequa River area suggest a Jurassic age for the Nu. The Napeequa unit may be the metamorphosed equivalent of the older part of the Hozameen Group; more specifically, the Twisp Valley Schist may be correlative with the Triassic upper chert-rich section of the Hozameen Group. The Hozameen Group are offset by the Straight Creek fault and form a Mississippian to Middle Jurassic terrane of greenstone and chert, with lesser amounts of limestone, argillite, gabbro, volcaniclastic sandstone, and serpentinite.
White to light-brown dacite tuff and welded tuff, some rhyolite tuff, and rare andesite tuff and flow rocks, commonly highly altered. Bedding obscure.

Pillow basalt, isolated pillow breccia, and mudflow breccia with minor interbeds of basaltic sandstone and siltstone and red calcareous argillite; pillows are commonly amygdaloidal and are porphyritic with phenocrysts of augite and plagioclase set in a fine-grained groundmass; pervasively sheared and laced with veins of laumontite, calcite, epidote, quartz, and prehnite; basalt correlates with the Crescent Formation north of the Crescent fault; coccoliths from calcareous argillite beds in the pillow lavas are assigned an early Eocene age.

Gray to tan to yellow-orange, poorly indurated siltstone, claystone, and sandstone; locally tuffaceous. Some sandstone beds are graded, cross-bedded, and cemented by iron oxides. The Latah Formation is defined as the lacustrine and fluvial sedimentary rocks interlayered with flows of the Columbia River Basalt Group in the northeastern part of the Columbia Basin. Exposures of the unit are present about 3 km southeast of Fort Spokane and about 5 km south of the mouth of Mill Canyon. The formation is commonly covered by talus from the overlying basalt. In some places the poorly indurated rocks have failed, causing the overlying basalt flow(s) to slide. Floral assemblages in the Latah Formation indicate a Miocene age.

Shallow marine and alluvial, volcanic-rich sandstone, siltstone, and shale. Locally highly fossiliferous. Plant remains common. Minor conglomerate predominantly consists of volcanic clasts, but locally contains chert pebbles.

Thick, laterally discontinuous, medium- to very coarse-grained, micaceous, feldspatholithic to lithofeldspathic sandstones separated by thin-bedded (1-12 in.) sandstone, siltstone, claystone, and shale; minor siltstone-, shale-, and slate-clast breccia, granule conglomerate, and pebble conglomerate; bedding of thick sandstones generally thicker than 3 ft; common platy shale, slate, or siltstone clasts; consists of part of the Hoh rock assemblage.

Metagabbro, metadiabase, and minor mafic metatonalite. Generally highly cataclastically deformed and altered to chlorite, epidote, albite, pumpellyite, and carbonate minerals. Many rocks with very fine grained high-relief minerals replacing plagioclase, probably pumpellyite and (or) lawsonite in fibrous matrix of green amphibole, chlorite, and epidote minerals. Grains are crushed, locally microbrecciated. Includes cataclastic tonalite northeast of Rockport.

Coarse-grained, equigranular biotite granite; color index of 3 to 5. The unit appears to grade into the migmatitic granodiorite of Gilbraltar Rock at the north end of Banks Lake, but contacts are poorly exposed and deeply weathered. The granite is believed to be part of the Keller Butte pluton and the Keller Butte Suite.

Granodiorite and granite similar to the Granodiorite and tonalite unit of the Index batholith but highly altered to sericite, epidote, and chlorite. Reported some micrographic and local granoblastic textures. Locally cataclastic. Contact breccias along margin are rich in clasts of volcanic rocks of Mount Persis.

Light gray, indurated, thin to thick-bedded and channeled, planar-laminated and graded to locally trough-laminated or cross-laminated, very fine to medium-grained micaceous feldspathic sandstone and well indurated, thin-bedded, dark-gray siltstone; contains foraminiferal faunas referable to the Ulatisian Stage; equivalent to Unit A of Wolfe and McKee (1972), lower McIntosh Formation of Wagner (1967a), sandstones of Megler, and sedimentary rocks of the Crescent Formation.  Breccia, conglomerate, volcanolithic sandstone, argillite, limestone, and chert; green, red, or black; chiefly basalt and diabase clasts; micaceous, carbonaceous, lithic, calcareous, and fossiliferous; interfingers with basaltic rocks.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Buffalo Hump Formation, Deer Trail Group
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Faintly to distinctly laminated argillite and phyllite. Light- to dark-gray, green and brown-green, but some is brown, maroon, black, and tan argillite. The argillite consists mostly of argillaceous or slatey rocks, but includes a range of lithologies. Argillite and phyllitic argillite at the base of the formation is greenish-gray to dark-gray and has even-parallel laminae and microlaminae. The amount of argillite is varied, but it is most abundant at the top and the base. Siltite is abundant in the transition zone between the argillite and the Buffalo Hump Formation quartzite. Bedding is typically not visible, but most rocks are thinly cleaved. Where cleavage can be distinguished from bedding, the cleavage angle differs from that of the underlying McHale Slate. Locally the absence of the argillite in the lower part of the Buffalo Hump Formation may be due to faulting, nondeposition, or an internal unconformity in the lower part of the formation The Buffalo Hump Formation is unconformably overlain by Windermere Group rocks or the Windermere Group rocks are thrust over the Buffalo Hump Formation. It is correlated with units C and D of the Striped Peak Formation in the Pend Oreille valley. The calculated maximum thickness for the formation in the central part of Huckleberry Mountain is 520 m and about 300 m on the hill north of the town of Valley.

Gray, medium- to coarse-grained, equigranular hornblende-biotite quartz monzodiorite and minor quartz diorite, ranging to granodiorite. Average composition is 50 percent plagioclase, 20 percent K-feldspar, 15 percent quartz, and 15 percent hornblende and biotite. Some of the hornblende crystals contain pyroxene cores. Accessory minerals include sphene, apatite, and magnetite.  The Swimptkin Creek pluton is generally massive, but it is locally foliated and lineated. The north-northwest-trending lineation is defined by the alignment of tabular hornblende crystals. It is parallel to the prominent lineation in the metamorphic rocks of the Okanogan metamorphic core complex. The pluton intrudes cataclastically deformed, amphibolite-facies metamorphic rocks of the Okanogan metamorphic core complex. Along the southern margin, the pluton has been cataclastically deformed along with the gneissic rocks that it intrudes. It intrudes the Tonasket Gneiss and the Crawfish Lake tonalite gneiss in the Okanogan metamorphic core complex. It contains inclusions and roof pendants of hornblende gabbro, diorite, mylonitic gneiss, and fine-grained hornfels. Metamorphic grade of the inclusions and pendants is sillimanite zone of the amphibolite facies. The inclusions may be banded gneisses (Tonasket Gneiss) of the Okanogan metamorphic core complex.

Fine to medium sand in active to stabilized, wind deposited dunes; predominantly composed of quartz and basalt grains derived from older sedimentary deposits. Stratification may be absent or may form broad, planar crossbeds; buried organic layers representing former soil horizons are locally present. Exposed thickness ranges from 1 m to more than 5 m.

Leucocratic, medium- to coarse-grained, biotite granodiorite to monzogranite that contains pink and white microcline phenocrysts as much as 7 to 8 cm long, euhedral biotite, subhedral to euhedral plagioclase, and anhedral quartz; accessory minerals include magnetite, sphene, apatite, zircon, and pyrite. Biotite content increases to the northeast. The unit is foliated at its eastern contact. This granite crops out between the middle fork of Mill Creek and the Little Pend Oreille River at the south edge of the Colville area. The contact metamorphic halo is approximately 1.5 km wide near Hande Creek where calc-silicate rock and amphibolite are present. Contacts with other intrusive rocks are unclear. The body has a groundmass texture similar to that of the Starvation Flat Quartz Monzonite and that the two plutons may be genetically related. However, the Starvation Flat unit contains hornblende and no microcline. A K-Ar age on biotite in this biotite granite is 104.5 +/- 2.9 Ma, indicating it is Cretaceous.

Dark-colored, massive to platy, porphyritic two pyroxene andesite and basaltic andesite flows and flow breccia; gray, porphyritic pyroxene basaltic andesite and minor andesite. In the Skate Creek and Butter Creek area, greenish to brownish-gray andesitic lavas form massive cliffs; at Skyo Mountain the unit consists chiefly of gray to brownish-green andesite flows and flow breccia with subordinate amounts of laharic and tuff-breccia. In the drainages of the North Fork Ahtanum Creek and South Fork Tieton River, poorly studied basaltic andesite lavas intercalated with well-bedded volcaniclastic rocks were considered to be Oligocene. Similar lavas have later been described as being similar to Fifes Peak Formation lavas. At American Ridge the unit consists of rocks described as overlying and underlying the tuff at Bumping River. Part of the unit has been referred to as Fifes Peak Formation at Union Creek, which consists of interstratified brown to grayish-green pyroxene andesite porphyry lava flows interstratified with light-colored volcaniclastic rocks. In a flow-dominated, homoclinally dipping sequence with minor interbedded volcaniclastic breccia and conglomerate in the Kiana Peak-Kiana Creek area. Believed to be equivalent to the Ohanapecosh lavas in Mount Rainier National Park; age dated near the upper part of the sequence at 27.0 +/- 1.8 m.y.b.p.

Ribbon chert with lesser pillow basalt, mafic tuff, limestone, and mudstone. Bedding, where preserved, is commonly contorted. Ribbon chert, which is commonly veined and fractured, is well bedded with shaly interbeds every few centimeters. Intraformational chert breccia and coarse chert-lithic sandstone occur locally. Pillow basalt and mafic tuff are interbedded with chert and are virtually identical to rocks of the Deadman Bay Volcanics, however, they are much less abundantly. Limestone is recrystallized into aragonite marble and is present as interbeds in chert and as olistolithic blocks. Interbedded mudstone and mafic tuff are locally abundant. Chert is light blue-gray to black (locally red), basalt and tuffs are green, limestone is gray to light pinkish gray, and mudstone is commonly black. Triassic to Early Jurassic ages were determined from radiolarians in chert. Recent collections have identified only Late Triassic (Norian) radiolarians. Limestone associated with chert yields Late Triassic conodonts. Brown and Vance (1987) consider this unit and the Deadman Bay Volcanics to be equivalent to the Elbow Lake Formation. The unit may locally include units of the Turtleback Complex of McLellan (1927) and the Constitution Formation of Vance (1975). Outcrops are found mainly on Orcas and Shaw Islands.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: mostly Vashon Stade in western WA; unnamed in eastern WA
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: A complex assemblage of (1) fossil-bearing stony silt, sand, and clay with associated layers, lenses, and pods of other diamictons and (2) medium- to well-sorted, massive to laminated sand, silt, and clay. Upper 1-2 m is commonly pale yellowish-brown (10YR 7/3-6/4) to dark grayish-brown (10YR 4/2); becomes gray (2.5Y 5) and less distinctly layered with depth. Thickness typically ranges from 1 to 10 m; exceptional thickness of approximately 15-18 m is found immediately east of the alluvial bottomland near Milltown, north of Stanwood, and in vicinity of Mt. Vernon. In the Stanwood-Mt. Vernon area, on northern and central Whidbey Island, and on San Juan and Lopez Islands, the unit includes discontinuous deposits of iron-stained, moderate- to well-sorted, locally fossiliferous sand and gravel that are interpreted as beach deposits associated with a former time of high relative sea level. The finer grained, more massive facies (2) typically has a well-developed vertically oriented columnar structure. Locally overlies or is interlayered with poorly sorted sand and gravel in which deformed bedding associated with ice-contact collapse is common. Topographic benches interpreted as wavecut terraces are also associated with the silt-clay deposits and with the inferred beach deposits. As mapped, includes the Everson Glaciomarine Drift of Eastebrook (1968)

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Alta Lake, amphibolite, schist, and gneiss of
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Banded heterogeneous, high-grade metamorphic rocks which forms discontinuous, well-layered, oxidized, sharply bounded bands. Schistose amphibolite intercalated with quartz-hornblende-plagioclase gneiss, leucocratic tonalitic gneiss, and minor hornblende-quartz-biotite-plagioclase schist, calc-silicate schist, and biotite-actinolite schist. The layered metamorphic rocks are cut by 0.3- to 5-m-thick trondhjemitic dikes and sills. Banding in the Alta Lake unit varies from planar to lenticular to discrete and is locally swirled near the migmatite. Nematoblastic hornblende prisms commonly define a lineation in the banded rocks that is, in most places, co-planar with the foliation. Tight to isoclinal folds are common; they are locally boudinaged. The Alta Lake metamorphic rocks are intruded by the Cooper Mountain batholith and the porphyry dike swarm of Goat Mountain. The long linear outcrop of the northern extension of the Alta Lake unit may be an oversimplification of discontinuous, discrete amphibolite bodies that define the linear trend. The amphibolite, schist, and gneiss of Alta Lake are intruded by the Cooper Mountain batholith and the porphyry dike swarm of Goat Mountain. The Methow Gneiss contains inclusions of the Alta Lake rocks, which suggests that the Methow Gneiss intruded the Alta Lake metamorphic rocks. Migmatitic zones 50-100 m wide are present at the contacts between the two units. Amphibolite in the Alta Lake unit has yielded a K-Ar hornblende age of 104 +/- 5 Ma; this is probably a metamorphic age. The amphibolite, schist, and gneiss of Alta Lake are correlative with the Leecher Metamorphics to the north on the Omak and Twisp areas, and may be correlative with the amphibolite and schist of Twentyfive Mile Creek to the west. These correlations would suggest an upper Paleozoic age (Permian) for the Alta Lake rocks, but they are shown as pre-Cretaceous because of the uncertainty of the correlations.

Only larger deposits are shown; mudflows mostly resulted from floods caused by eruptions on Mount Rainier volcano, but some probably originated during periods of unusually heavy rainfall; mudflows are interbedded with alluvium in terraces or benches in the Pyramid Creek-Kautz Creek drainage and upper Nisqually River valley and the upper reaches of the Ohanapecosh River valley; mudflows are generally younger than 6,600 yr.

Black to dark-gray-green, massive to vesicular, aphyric to porphyritic, clinopyroxene and olivine-augite basalt flows and flow breccia; similar in appearance to the lower Miocene andesite and basaltic andesite flows unit at Lone Tree Mountain, but chemical analyses reveal a slightly less silicic composition (49-53 percent SiO2); locally includes interbedded mafic tuff, lahars, and minor sedimentary rocks; basalt flows and flow breccias form a broad shield volcano, centered just south of Huffaker Mountain K-Ar age dated (plagioclase) at 23.2 +/- 0.7 m.y. B.P.

Poorly to moderately sorted arkose to subarkosic quartz-feldspar-bearing wacke and quartz-bearing arenite with intercalated greenstone, metabasalt, phyllite, metawacke, carbonate, argillite, conglomerate, and basaltic greenstone. Light- to medium-gray, well-bedded to massive limestone, dolomite, and impure marble.  The Covada Group crops out along both sides of the Columbia River (Roosevelt Lake). It extends south into the Nespelem area, where it forms a broad south-trending belt. Three locations of limestone in the Covada Group have been identified: (1) Medium-gray and recrystallized limestone in 1- to 10-m-thick lenses in the eastern part of the Covada Group. The lenses, which are sandy in places and have phyllitic partings, are in the greenstone unit and at the contacts of the greenstone with metasedimentary rocks. (2) Carbonate along Jones Creek that ranges from massive, fetid, limestone and dolomite in the western part to calcareous phyllite to the east. Contacts with the adjacent siliciclastic rocks of the Covada Group are poorly preserved and not well understood. This large carbonate body is in probable fault contact with higher grade metamorphic rocks to the south, and may stratigraphically overlie or interfinger with metasedimentary rocks of the Covada Group to the east. (3) White to gray marble and gray to greenish calc-silicate rocks with wollastonite and pyrite interbedded with thin-bedded, medium-gray, argillaceous calcite marble adjacent to the porphyritic granodiorite of Manila Creek. The contact between the Covada Group and amphibolite-facies metamorphic rocks in the Kettle metamorphic core complex is probably a low-angle normal fault. A fault also separates the Covada Group from the Paleozoic(?) metasedimentary rocks at Heidegger Hill. Few fossils have been found in the Covada Group, but Early to early Late Ordovician macrofossils and conodonts have been recovered from the rocks in the Nespelem area. Older metasedimentary rocks and greenstone of the Covada Group are present on the Colville Indian Reservation, and were also mapped on the east side of the Columbia River. The Covada Group was correlated with Carboniferous sedimentary rocks from Alaska to California. Plant fossils, reported to be from the Covada Group near the Silver Leaf mine, were described to be of Pennsylvanian(?) age.  Basaltic greenstones and a probable fault-bounded lens of quartzo-feldspathic wacke and arenite in the Kettle Falls, Republic and Colville area are correlated with the Covada Group. The Covada Group is also correlated with the Lardeau Group in southern British Columbia and the Valmy Formation in the Roberts Mountains Allochthon in Nevada.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Grande Ronde Basalt, R2, Columbia River Basalt
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Dark gray to black, medium- to very fine grained, aphyric to very sparsely plagioclase-phyric basaltic andesite. Nonporphyritic. Groundmass textures dominantly intersertal, with small clots of plagioclase and clinopyroxene. Pillows, hyaloclastites, and invasive flows common. Locally includes thin sedimentary deposits of the Ellensburg Formation. Possesses uniform lithologic and petrologic characteristics. Divisible informally on the basis of MgO content and paleomagnetic polarity. Magnetostratigraphic units present are: N(2) magnetostratigraphic unit and R(2) magnetostratigraphic unit. The Grande Ronde Basalt formation has at least 120 flows are known; these are divided into 17 informal units. Further is divided into four magnetostratigraphic units. Upper four or five flows of this unit are high-Mg Grande Ronde chemical type; commonly microphyric with 1- to 3-mm-long equant plagioclase phenocrysts. Lower flows of this unit are low-Mg Grande Ronde chemical type; fine-grained; aphyric; thick, massive, hackly entablatures over colonnades. Discontinuous, invaded sedimentary interbeds common near top and bottom of this sequence of flows. The dense to slightly vesicular flows are of normal magnetic polarity. Chemically, flows of the Grande Ronde Basalt are tholeiitic basalt (basaltic andesite). The unit makes up 87 percent of the volume of the Columbia River Basalt Group (CRBG). The groundmass contains plagioclase, augite, and pigeonite. Plagioclase phenocrysts are sparse and microphenocrysts of orthopyroxene, pigeonite, and olivine are rare. Abundant disseminated magnetite and/or ilmenite. In the Blue Mountains, the Grande Ronde has a maximum aggregate thickness of more than 1,235 m, and the maximum thickness exposed at a single locality is about 1,050 m. In the BN 1-9 borehole on the Saddle Mountains, the base of the Grande Ronde Basalt was encountered at approximately 3,500 m drilled depth, making the Grande Ronde Basalt approximately 3,200 m thick. Flows of the Grande Ronde Basalt were erupted between about 15.5 m.y. and about 16.5 m.y. ago.

An assemblage of metadiorite, meta-quartz diorite, metagabbro, and minor amphibolite that is riddled with small bodies of directionless, leucocratic quartz monzonite and granodiorite. The metadiorite, meta-quartz diorite, metagabbro, and amphibolite in the Tiffany complex are directionless to weakly foliated, fine- to coarse-grained rocks composed of plagioclase (labradorite-andesine), hornblende, biotite, and minor quartz. Accessory minerals include apatite, magnetite, sphene, and epidote. Mafic minerals typically form 20-35 percent of the rocks. Microscopic textures in the metadiorite, meta-quartz diorite, and metagabbro show a progressive development from granoblastic to porphyroblastic to igneous-appearing, suggesting formation by recrystallization. The composition of the rocks and the presence of minor amphibolite bodies within them suggest derivation from an amphibolitic source rock. The absence of layering in the rocks indicates a derivation from basic igneous material rather than from basic sediments. The leucocratic quartz monzonite and granodiorite in the Tiffany complex are directionless, medium- to coarse-grained rocks composed of quartz, microcline, plagioclase, biotite, and hornblende. Mafic minerals generally form less than 10 percent of rocks. Microcline is commonly perthitic and plagioclase, is locally antiperthitic, indicating that microcline has replaced plagioclase. The leucocratic quartz monzonite and granodiorite form dike-like bodies and small masses within the metadiorite, metaquartz diorite, and metagabbro. Uniform compositions of the quartz monzonite and granodiorite bodies over wide areas and sharp contacts between the leucocratic rocks and the metadioritic rocks suggest that the leucocratic rocks intruded the metadioritic rocks. Crystalloblastic textures in the leucocratic rocks indicate that intrusion occurred before or during recrystallization of the metadioritic rocks. The Tiffany complex forms a 60-square kilometers, northwest-trending mass between Muckamuck Pass (T. 36 N., R. 24 E.) and Rock Mountain (T. 37 N., R. 23 E.). The complex is intruded by the Conconully and Bottle Spring plutons. It grades into the gneissic trondhjemite of Tiffany Mountain and the Leader Mountain granodioritic gneiss. The contact with the metamorphic complex of Conconully to the east is sharp. The absence of a strong structural fabric in the Tiffany complex suggests that it formed after regional dynamothermal metamorphism of the metamorphic complex of Conconully. Therefore, a Cretaceous or Jurassic age is suspected.

Melanocratic diorite gneiss forms a north-south belt in the Coyote Ridge quartz diorite gneiss, parallel to the thrust fault along the western margin of the Summit-Frazer trondhjemitic gneiss. The rocks consist of hornblende, biotite, feldspar, and quartz. The constituents are locally segregated into leucocratic and melanocratic bands. The amphibolite near Finley Canyon is strongly deformed. Mylonitic foliation, isoclinal intrafolial folds, box folds, and brittle faults are all common. Some fractures are filled with epidote; epidote is also present in some of the rock as a retrograde metamorphic mineral.

A central phase of medium- to coarse-grained, porphyritic granodiorite and quartz monzonite  and a border phase of fine-grained, equigranular mesocratic monzonite and quartz diorite. The porphyritic granodiorite and quartz monzonite are composed of euhedral microperthitic microcline crystals, as much as 5 cm across, in a medium- to coarse-grained groundmass of plagioclase (oligoclase-albite), microcline, and quartz. Some of the anhedral quartz crystals are clustered together, forming small glomerocrysts. Biotite, chlorite, epidote, and magnetite are the chief mafic minerals. They are commonly intergrown, forming masses that are apparently pseudomorphous after hornblende. A few relict hornblende crystals are also present. Sphene and epidote are common accessory minerals. The mesocratic monzonite and quartz diorite are compositionally similar to the porphyritic rocks, except that they contain less microcline and quartz and more hornblende and biotite. The equigranular, mesocratic rocks are cut by the porphyritic rocks in places, indicating that the border phase is older. The Whisky Mountain pluton is a 15-square kilometer, northwest-trending, elongate intrusion between Wannacut Lake and the Okanogan River valley north of Ellisforde (T. 38 and 39 N., R. 27 E.). Igneous textures dominate the pluton. Most of the rocks are directionless, but a weak foliation is locally developed along the borders of the intrusion. The southeastern part of the pluton, east of the Okanogan River, has been cataclastically deformed along the Okanogan fault. The Whisky Mountain pluton intrudes the Permian Anarchist Group. Hornblende from mesocratic quartz diorite near the center of the pluton yielded a K-Ar age of 119 +/- 5 Ma. However, because much of the pluton has been strongly altered, it is unlikely that this radiometric age represents the magmatic crystallization age.

A layered sequence of phyllite, greenstone, and quartzite (metachert). The unit forms a broad, discontinuous belt along the Canadian border between Chopaka Mountain (T. 40 N., R. 25 E.) and Chesaw (T. 40 N., R. 30 E.). The Kobau Formation is approximately 650 m thick on Ellemeham Mountain northeast of Palmer Lake. Along the Canadian border, the Kobau Formation consists of grayish-green phyllite and subordinate quartzite, greenstone, and metalimestone. The black and bluish-gray quartzite consists chiefly of fine-grained quartz, with minor actinolite, mica, and other metamorphic minerals. It is thought to have formed by recrystallization of chert, not elastic quartzose sandstone. The thinly layered to massive greenstone is generally aphanitic, but is locally porphyritic. Metalimestone layers are typically fine-grained and dolomitic. The Kobau Formation(?) also form isolated outcrops on the southern end of Duffys Mountain (T. 37 N., R. 27 E.), along the southwest side of Cayuse Mountain (T. 37 N., R. 26 E.), and 3 km southwest of Janis (sec. 12, T. 36 N., R. 26 E.). At these localities, the formation consists of interbedded greenish-gray phyllite, greenstone, amphibolite, and minor massive light-gray metadolomite and metalimestone with sparse chert nodules. The amphibolite and greenstone are weakly foliated to directionless, fine- to medium-grained rocks composed chiefly of actinolite and chlorite. They generally form concordant layers a few tens of meters thick, but also occur as discontinuous, irregularly shaped masses. The fine-grained greenstone probably represents lava flows and pyroclastic rocks, and the medium-grained amphibolite may represent hypabyssal intrusions. Magnesitic metadolomite and serpentinite form discontinuous lenses in the Kobau Formation along the Similkameen River (sec. 18, T. 40 N., R. 27 E.) and east of Chesaw. It is believed that the magnesitic rocks are sedimentary in origin. The serpentinite formed by alteration of the magnesitic rocks. Others believe that the magnesitic rocks formed by alteration of serpentinite. The magnesitic rocks and serpentinite lie along a regional thrust fault that separates the Kobau Formation from the Anarchist Group. The Kobau Formation is equivalent to the Kobau Group in southern British Columbia. It is intruded by the Similkameen and Loomis plutons and by the Late Triassic orthogneiss of Osoyoos. The Kobau Formation conformably overlies, grades into, and is locally intruded by the Palmer Mountain Greenstone. It is unconformably overlain by the Ellemeham Formation, which is probably Early Jurassic in age. It is thought that the Kobau Formation unconformably overlies the Permian Anarchist Group. It is also believed that the contact between the two units is marked by a regional thrust fault. Because no fossils have been recovered from the Kobau Formation, and because the nature of the contact between the Kobau Formation and the Anarchist Group is uncertain, the age of the Kobau Formation is unknown. However, because it is intruded by the orthogneiss of Osoyoos (200 Ma), the Kobau Formation must be Triassic or older.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Wingate Hill Drift, till deposits of
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Present in a small upland area south of the Puyallup River and in the hills east of Salkum (3.2 km west of Mayfield Lake); average thickness of weathered rinds on stones is 4 mm (ranging from 1 to 8 mm).

Olivine basalt. The lava was erupted from a vent at Red Butte on the northeast flank of Mount Adams and flowed along the Clearwater Creek and Trappers Creek drainages. The cone at the vent consists of scoria and agglutinate. The unit has a Holocene age.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Andesite and basaltic-andesite flows and flow breccia
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Porphyritic pyroxene andesite and basaltic-andesite flows and flow breccia, locally includes minor basalt and dacite flows, breccia, and interbedded volcaniclastic rocks; typically consists of plagioclase, augite, and hypersthene phenocrysts in pilotaxitic groundmass of plagioclase, pyroxene, magnetite, quartz, and interstitial glass (usually altered to fine-grained smectite); includes hypabyssal sills or dikes in areas where contacts could not be observed.

Sandstone, shale, and conglomerate. White to buff- gray, medium- to coarse-grained, micaceous, feldspathic to lithofeldspathic sandstone. Composition averages 35 to 40 percent quartz, 45 to 50 percent feldspar, and 10 to 15 percent lithic clasts of which 90 percent are volcanic rock; also includes lesser amounts of interbedded pebbly sandstone, conglomerate, and minor shale. Massive red to purple and green conglomerate in beds 6 m thick with 1- to 2-m thick dark-colored sandstone interbeds. Clasts are quartz diorite, phyllite and chert, as in other conglomerate, and amygdaloidal basalt and rhyolite.Sedimentary structures include graded, crossbedded and channeled sandstone, and imbricate pebbles in conglomerate. Angular to subrounded clasts of biotite gneiss and vein quartz in a matrix of reddish sandstone, exposed mostly near the gneissic core of the Eagle Creek anticline.

Thick to thin bedded; friable, very fine to medium grained, micaceous, [feldspathic] sandstone and silty sandstone; plane laminated thin bedded micaceous siltstone, some with large, low-angle cross-bedding sets; large channels in siltstone filled with very coarse sand and transported blocks of siltstone; convolute bedding and slump structures common.

Leucocratic, coarse-grained, porphyritic, foliated, muscovite-biotite granodiorite. Quartz is light gray and forms clusters of rounded, granular crystals that are stretched parallel to biotite. The average biotite:muscovite ratio is approximately 5:1. The muscovite content increases and the biotite:muscovite ratio decreases toward the center of the body. Muscovite and biotite are subhedral and similar in size and mode of occurrence. This unit is cut by alaskite pegmatite dikes, and it intrudes rocks of the Windermere and Priest River Groups. Metamorphic effects extend approximately 1 km from the contact.

Narrow (1-km-wide) fault-bounded block of pillowed greenstones with rare shale interbeds (fault slices?); strongly resemble greenstones within the Russell Ranch unit and may be correlative; unit is found as a long continuous outcrop belt interrupted only by Cenozoic rocks, unlike the small discontinuous tectonic blocks within elastic rocks of the clastic subunit of the Russell Ranch; sedimentary interbeds are rare in this unit but are common in the tectonic blocks of pillowed greenstone in elastic subunit of Russell Ranch unit; unit consists almost entirely of pillowed flows, whereas in the tectonic blocks of pillowed greenstone in elastic subunit of Russell Ranch unit, both pillowed and massive flows are abundant; metamorphic grade of the eastern greenstone unit is slightly less than that of the tectonic blocks of pillowed greenstone in elastic subunit of Russell Ranch unit; age of Cretaceous-Jurassic(?) is tentatively assigned based on unit's weak association with the tectonic blocks of pillowed greenstone in elastic subunit of Russell Ranch unit; consists of part of the Russell Ranch Formation.

Massive, dark-green to black, plagioclase-porphyritic two-pyroxene andesite and andesitic breccia and tuff; includes dense aphanitic to fine-grained basalt and coarse-grained gabbro. Phenocrysts and glomerocrysts of plagioclase, clinopyroxene, hypersthene, mostly greatly altered in an intersertal to holocrystalline groundmass of mainly clinopyroxene, plagioclase, and opaque minerals. Black basalt is aphyric to microporphyritic, commonly trachytoid, and locally with altered olivine. Upper part of unit includes rare interbedded, dark-gray to brownish volcanic sandstone and siltstone. Generally poorly indurated volcanic sandstone contains angular to rounded clasts of volcanic rocks, altered glass, and plagioclase crystals; also contains clasts of chert, sandstone, and siltstone. Variably altered to smectites, epidote, and calcite. Locally hornfelsic near Tertiary plutons, most extensively south of Youngs Creek stock. Near Calligan Lake, unit includes andesite and dacite porphyry dike swarm.
Light- to medium-gray andesite forming thick (20 to 22 m) glaciated and forested lava flows; age preglacial (older than about 10,000 yr).

Several flows of dark-gray hypersthene-augite phyric andesite and at least one flow of olivine andesite erupted from vents southwest of Pinegrass Ridge, which were the center of the Plio-Pleistocene Goat Rocks stratovolcano. One of the least altered lavas of the Goat Rocks volcano. Partly fill a deep canyon eroded by Tieton River into Grande Ronde Basalt and Fifes Peak Formation and advanced downstream as far as the mouth of Cowiche Canyon. One flow, up to 120 m thick, extends down the Tieton River canyon to Naches, nearly 80 km from its probable source in the Goat Rocks area. Remnants remarkably columnar in places.

Serpentinite, talc-magnesite schist, talc schist, tremolite-talc schist, and olivine-talc rocks. Thick, large layers along Downey Creek are mostly metadunite. Other bodies are serpentinized metadunite and metaperidotite. The large body on Jordan Creek is mostly serpentinized peridotite.  Predominantly fine-grained hornblende-mica schist, mica-quartz schist, hornblende schist, amphibolite, garnet-biotite schist, and minor hornblende-zoisite schist, hornblende garbenschiefer, calc-silicate schist, marble, and ultramafic rocks. Rocks are dark green to black on fresh surfaces, weathering rusty orange to brown with relics of olivine in a felted mat of antigorite, talc, and tremolite. In the Cascade River area and in the Straight Creek Fault zone, phyllitic muscovite-chlorite-quartz schist predominates. Rocks are mostly white, tan, brown to black, locally greenish with conspicuous compositional banding. Fine lamellar foliation, locally blastomylonitic. On outcrop scale the schist is isoclinally folded, commonly crenulated; small crinkle folds of prominent foliation surfaces.  Larger bodies and masses along the Entiat fault are serpentine and serpentinized metaperidotite; smaller bodies and pods elsewhere are mostly talc schist and tremolite-talc rock, commonly highly foliate.

Graphitic sericite-plagioclase-quartz phyllite and semischistose lithic-volcanic subquartzose sandstone. Protolith sediments thin to medium bedded. Locally highly contorted, but generally lacks prominent multiple crenulations characteristic of the Darrington Phyllite.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Hobuck Lake, sedimentary and basaltic rocks of
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Thin-bedded siltstone with interbedded basaltic tuff-breccia and quartzose sandstone; overlain by mudflow deposits, pillow lava, and breccia. Thin- and wispy-bedded tuffaceous siltstone with interbedded basaltic fine tuff to tuff-breccia and thin-bedded to massive siltstone with thin quartzose sandstone interbeds; includes several massive to thick-bedded, quartzose, lithofeldspathic sandstone beds (1-5 m thick) along the outcrop area.

Light-gray, nonporphyritic, very coarse to coarse-grained, equigranular biotite quartz monzonite that is generally restricted to the border phase. Quartz is anhedral; K-feldspar is orthoclase. Plagioclase is zoned and unzoned; cores average An47. Myrmekite is common around plagioclase. Biotite forms subhedral books, and it is foliated near the borders of the pluton. Accessory minerals include apatite, sphene, magnetite, hematite, allanite, zircon, and hornblende. East-west elongate, undeformed, biotite quartz monzonite, granite, and monzogranite. The pluton is thought to be a magmatic differentiate with two phases: a central porphyritic biotite granite and a nonporphyritic biotite quartz monzonite border phase. A small late-phase alaskitic body is also present. A biotite-hornblende quartz diorite and gabbro was thought to be the oldest phase of the pluton. However, petrographic evidence led to the conclusion that this rock, at the eastern margin of the pluton, was in fact Precambrian amphibolite intruded and partially assimilated by the porphyritic monzogranite. The pluton is intruded by lamprophyre dikes, mineralized quartz veins, aplite, and pegmatite dikes. The pluton has sharp intrusive contacts with border rocks. Contact metamorphism has affected all metasedimentary and metavolcanic rocks along its border. The inner metamorphic aureole of the Spirit pluton was assigned to the hornblende-hornfels facies. Carbonate rocks of the Metaline Formation 3 m or closer to the pluton contain an assemblage of diopside, calcite, wollastonite +/- idocrase +/- forsterite(?) +/- garnet; at distances of more than 3 m and less than 100 m, a common assemblage in the Metaline is tremolite, diopside, and quartz. At distances of 100 m to 600 m from the border of the pluton the assemblage of tremolite, calcite, and quartz is common in these carbonate rocks. Pelitic Precambrian rocks on Huckleberry Mountain 3 m or closer to the border of the pluton contain an assemblage of quartz, biotite, muscovite +/- cordierite +/- andalusite. Biotite from the nonporphyritic border phase at the west end of the pluton gave a K-Ar age of 102 +/- 2.8 Ma. Hornblende from the quartz diorite, which is thought to be an assimilated amphibolite, was given an age of 96.3 +/- 3.0 Ma. Nearly west-trending structures probably controlled the emplacement of the pluton; the pluton clearly crosscuts folding.
Cobble and sand outwash deposits forming dissected terraced deposits along the Lewis River valley

Monolithologic breccia composed of angular sandstone clasts as much as 10 m across, derived from the Swauk Formation. Rare volcanic clasts. East of Spade Lake, breccia is locally highly sheared and altered. Basal sandstone breccia with lapilli tuff matrix has been described.

Light-gray, phyric, hypersthene andesite. Dense, fine-grained, and platy jointed flows are 2-10 m thick. The cumulative thickness is 80 m, and the approximate volume is about 0.23 km3. The source of these flows is probably buried by younger andesite flows from Mount Adams. The andesite of Swampy Meadow may be an early flow from Mount Adams.

Thick to thin-bedded, very fine to medium-grained, plane laminated, carbonaceous, micaceous, friable sandstone; basalt and quartzite conglomerate lenses locally common; bioturbated and containing slumped structures in places; molluscan fauna referred to Newportian or Pillarian Stages; includes part of lower Astoria Formation of Wolfe and McKee (1968).

Light-gray, sparsely phyric, olivine basalt. Olivine phenocrysts are set in a pilotaxitic groundmass of primarily plagioclase and olivine. The basalt forms blocky jointed lava flows, 4-12 m thick, with scoriaceous zones separating individual flows. The maximum cumulative thickness is 73 m, and the volume is approximately 11.5 km3. This unit forms the basal part of the Lemei Rock volcano and is stratigraphically confined to be about 200,000 to 500,000 yr b.p.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Box Canyon, intrusive diabase and basalt of
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Tabular intrusive complex of diabase sills in Box Canyon on southeast side of Mount Rainier; dark-colored porphyritic augite diabase that is propylitically altered; 8 km long by 300 m thick; major complex emplaced along contact between Stevens Ridge and Ohanapecosh Formations; swarms of basalt dikes of the same composition as the sills crop out in the area.
Mostly porphyritic biotite-hornblende tonalite to hornblende tonalite porphyry. Rocks are quartz-phyric with hypidiomorphic granular groundmass, but heterogeneous in grain size and texture.

Biotite-hornblende tonalite with Color Index=20-35. Subidiomorphic granular to crystalloblastic gneissose. Faint relict euhedral oscillatory zoning in plagioclase. Locally poikiloblastic hornblende prisms are well aligned. Rock is altered to epidote, chlorite, and prehnite.

Mostly fine- to medium-grained well-laminated mica schist similar to the Biotite schist of the Chiwaukum Schist but with rare to abundant schistose amphibolite, fine-grained hornblende gneiss, and less common calc-silicate schist and marble. Cut by dikes and sills of light-colored biotite tonalite and pegmatite. Grades into gneiss, schist, and amphibolite, banded gneiss.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Priest River Group, calc-silicate rock of
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: The character of the unit depends on the degree of metamorphism and its original composition. In the Harvey Creek area the most common rock types are interlayered white, fine-grained quartzite and brown, white, and pale-green calc-silicate rock. Plagioclase, actinolite, tremolite, and garnet are the most common calc-silicate minerals. The unit includes thick zones of impure marble. Locally, where thermal metamorphism is less intense but dynamic metamorphism is strong, chlorite-bearing phyllite is interlayered with highly cleaved tremolite marble and fine-grained quartzite. Brown layers, which were apparently argillite, are metamorphosed to fine-grained quartz-plagioclase-biotite rock. Layering is S2; all bedding has been destroyed by slip cleavage prior to or during metamorphism. On Hande Creek, east-northeast of Colville, impure marbles, calc-silicate rock, and hornfels are interbedded with phyllite, quartzite, and schist. Marble is white to green to light gray and has green and tan, contorted bands, which in places contain chlorite, wollastonite, diopside, garnet, and calcite. The contact with the overlying Leola Volcanics is covered; amphibolite float is present adjacent to calc-silicate outcrops.

Massive granodiorite, quartz monzonite, and monzonite, typically medium to coarse grained and porphyritic, but non-porphyritic varieties also are present, particularly near the center of the pluton. The porphyritic rocks are composed of scattered tabular phenocrysts of microperthitic microcline, as much as 2 cm long, in a medium-grained groundmass of plagioclase, K-feldspar, quartz, hornblende, biotite, and epidote. Hornblende crystals commonly contain pyroxene cores. Sphene and zircon are common accessory minerals. With the exception of the lack of microcline phenocrysts, the non-porphyritic rocks are petrographically similar to the porphyritic rocks. The central phase forms more than 90 percent of the Similkameen pluton. A progressive decrease in quartz content toward the margins of the central phase has resulted in a crude zonation from quartz monzonite to granodiorite to monzonite. The monzonite grades into malignite-shonkinite along the borders of the pluton. Dikes and irregular masses of alaskite cut both the central phase granitic rocks and the border phase alkalic rocks. The alaskite bodies sharply crosscut the other rocks, indicating they were intruded after solidification of the main mass of the pluton. The fine- to medium-grained alaskite consists of oligoclase, microcline, quartz, and accessory muscovite, biotite, sphene, magnetite, zircon, apatite, and garnet. The Similkameen pluton is a 350-square kilometers, east-trending, oval intrusion that straddles the Canadian border along the Similkameen River (T. 40 N., R. 23 to 26 E.). The pluton is a concentrically zoned intrusion, composed of a central phase of quartz monzonite, granodiorite, and monzonite, and a discontinuous border phase of mesocratic shonkinite, nepheline syenite, pyroxenite, and minor malignite. Dikes and irregular bodies of alaskite cut both the central and border phases in places, but cut only the border phase in other places. Cross-cutting relations suggest that the order of intrusion was: (1) pyroxenite; (2) malignite-shonkinite; (3) nepheline syenite; (4) monzonite-granodiorite-quartz monzonite; and (5) alaskite. The Similkameen pluton intrudes the Chopaka intrusive complex, the Kobau Formation, and the heterogeneous metamorphic rocks near Toats Coulee Creek. Contacts with the country rocks are generally sharp and discordant. Several strongly discordant K-Ar ages and a Rb-Sr isochron age of 170 +/- 5 Ma are reported from the Similkameen pluton. A concordant U-Pb zircon age of 170 +/- 2 Ma is reported from granodiorite along the northern border of the pluton near Keremeos, British Columbia.

Granodiorite, quartz diorite, and gabbro; unmetamorphosed or slightly metamorphosed; exposed in a small area; Cretaceous or Jurassic age assigned because this unit is slightly metamorphosed and intrudes Triassic and Jurassic rocks.
Basaltic, andesitic, or dacitic rocks; medium dark gray to dark greenish gray; porphyritic.

South of the Cowlitz River, light- to dark-gray, hypersthene andesite, hypersthene basaltic andesite, and two-pyroxene basaltic andesite flows and flow breccia; fresh-looking, platy, non-vesicular flows occasionally displaying columnar jointing; interbedded with tan to dark brown basaltic andesitic clast- and matrix-supported volcanic breccia in the Hiawatha syncline south of Alder Lake; lower Miocene(?) age assigned to this unit on the basis of two K-Ar age dates: (1) 20.7 +/- 0.3 m.y.b.p., (2) 23.2+/- 1.7 m.y.b.p..

Medium-grained hornblende-biotite tonalite and biotite tonalite fine-to medium-grained, rarely pegmatitic, tonalite-trondhjemite cut by dikes of various compositions; exhibiting inequigranular and hypidiomorphic texture; subordinate hornblende-biotite-tonalite schlieren. Consists of oligoclase, quartz, unzoned andesine (An38+/-2), muscovite, and biotite (partially altered to chlorite). Potassium feldspar is rare, but locally the concentration warrants a granodiorite classification. Accessory minerals include apatite, zircon, carbonate, titanite, and opaque minerals. At Bald Butte, this unit has a crystallization order of hornblende-biotite-tonalite (first), biotite-tonalite, aplite dikes, quartz-gabbro dikes, pegmatite dikes, and quartz dikes (last). Weak foliation dips steeply and trends approximately east or parallel to the ridge of Bald Butte. A sample from the Chambers Road-U.S. Highway 195 junction yields a K-Ar age of 69.8 +/- 2.6 Ma. A pegmatite vein thought to be related to this tonalite cuts quartzite south of Moscow, ID.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Portage Head/Point of Arches block, conglomerate and breccia of
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Thick- to medium- bedded, medium-grained, quartzose, concretionary, carbonaceous lithic sandstone with thin siltstone interbeds; on north side of Portage Head, contains a few interbeds of basaltic lapilli-tuff and chert-bearing volcanic pebble conglomerate; probably correlates with thick-bedded quartzose lithic sandstone; siltstone interbeds contain foraminifera assigned to the Ulatisian Stage.

Biotite metatonalite with relict hypidiomorphic granular texture. Biotite metatonalite, based on modes, but rocks are granodiorite based on cation norms and delta oxygen-18 values greater than 10. Relict hypidiomorphic granular texture with plagioclase mostly filled with well-crystallized epidote and muscovite; some crushed grain margins have recrystallized, and quartz is sutured. Some K-feldspar is microcline. Rocks are massive and sharply intrusive.

Distinctly layered hornblende diorite, with layers defined by variation in relative proportions of hornblende and plagioclase. Hornblende content varies from 20 to 70 percent. The age of this small intrusion on the ridge separating Middle and Grizzly Creeks (sec. 32, T. 39 N., R. 16 E.), along the western margin of the Methow basin is unknown. It is compositionally similar to, and probably correlative with, the Lightning Creek stocks. Therefore, a Late Cretaceous age is suspected.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Copper Peak and Holden Lake plutons
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Dark gray (Color Index 40-50), medium-grained, massive, hypidiomorphic to panidiomorphic granular quartz diorite to tonalite, with lesser quartz gabbro. Minerals include plagioclase (labradorite), hornblende, and quartz. Some hornblende has augite cores; magnetite commonly makes up 5 percent of the rock, and apatite and titanite are accessory. The parallel orientation of labradorite suggests platonic flow alignment. The Holden Lake pluton has low silicon content and high ferromagnesian mafic mineral content and has some tholeiitic chemical characteristics. The unit forms numerous dikes and elongate masses about 2.5 km east of Holden Lake. The largest intrusions have a width of about 1.5 km and are at least 2 km long. The Copper Peak pluton crops out on the north side of Copper Peak and is a little more than 1.5 km long and about 0.5 km wide, although dikes of the rock are widespread as much as 1.5 km farther west. Contacts are typically sharp, except where locally sharp contacts give way to spectacular contact complexes. These plutons are cut by the late Eocene Duncan Hill pluton and are thus older. But, because the satellitic dikes cut mineralized rock associated with the Duncan Hill pluton, the unit is assigned a late Eocene age.

Nonvolcanic conglomerate with locally derived clasts. The unit is present west of Colville and near Williams Lake. In the Williams Lake area most of the unit is megabreccia derived from the Spirit pluton. There, the unit is overlain by water-laid tuffaceous sandstone and cut by shonkinite and hypabyssal dikes. The conglomerate is a distinct unit, stratigraphically below the O'Brien Creek Formation, but has been correlated with the O'Brien Creek Formation. Near Gold Creek this unit is mapped as the lower conglomerate and contains rounded to subangular clasts of quartzite, argillite, chert-pebble conglomerate, wacke, limestone, and granitic rock in a yellowish-brown sandstone matrix which includes coarse-grained to pebble-size angular fragments of argillite. The unit is estimated to be 183 m thick. A thin tuff is present at the top of the conglomerate.

Poorly to moderately sorted arkose to subarkosic quartz-feldspar-bearing wacke and quartz-bearing arenite with intercalated greenstone, carbonate, argillite, conglomerate, basaltic greenstone, phyllite, and slate. Fine- to coarse-grained, gray, greenish-gray, and tan, impure quartzite and wacke (greater than 10 percent argillaceous matrix). Most quartzite and wacke are quartzofeldspathic and have abundant to sparse lithic fragments; other constituents include muscovite, biotite, tourmaline, zircon, and varied amounts of opaque minerals. Most lithic fragments and mineral grains are subangular to subrounded. Locally, quartzite is well sorted, vitreous, and quartz-rich. Phyllite and argillite is dominantly dark-gray to black, thinly foliated. Layering in the argillite and phyllite is commonly distorted by minor isoclinal and disharmonic folds. Phyllite is composed of muscovite, biotite, quartz, and feldspar, and it is commonly spotted with chlorite porphyroblasts. Most limestone is interbedded with the finer grained rocks and is dark, fine grained, and impure; however, some limestone is white, coarsely crystalline, and pure. Greenstone layers are generally thin (approximately 1 m) thick. Near the contact between the Covada Group and the amphibolite-facies rocks in the Kettle metamorphic core complex, the Covada Group consists of massive, fine- to medium-grained, poorly sorted quartzite that is composed chiefly of subrounded quartz grains. The Covada Group has been subdivided into greenstone, carbonate rock, and wacke units. A heterogeneous assemblage of phyllite, argillite, quartzite, metawacke, metalimestone, and minor greenstone and metabasalt, crops out along both sides of the Columbia River (Roosevelt Lake). It extends south into the Nespelem area, where it forms a broad south-trending belt. The contact between the Covada Group and amphibolite-facies metamorphic rocks in the Kettle metamorphic core complex to the west is probably a low-angle normal fault. A fault also separates the Covada Group from the Paleozoic(?) metasedimentary rocks at Heidegger Hill. Trilobites from limestone interbedded with greenstone indicate an Early Ordovician age for at least that part of the unit. Plant fossils, reported to be from the Covada Group near the Silver Leaf mine, to be of Pennsylvanian(?) age. Metasedimentary rocks and greenstone on the east side of the Columbia River were mapped and correlated with similar rocks mapped as Covada Group by Pardee (1918). The Covada Group is correlated with the Lardeau Group in southern British Columbia and the Valmy Formation in the Roberts Mountains Allochthon in Nevada, which also contain texturally mature quartz arenite and arkosic sediments. Basaltic greenstones and a probable fault-bounded lens of quartzo-feldspathic wacke and arenite in the Kettle Falls area on the Republic and Colville areas are also correlated with the Covada Group. U/Pb dating of detrital zircons suggests a heterogenous early Proterozoic source area for the coarse elastics in the Covada Group. The Castle Rock Creek-Mitre Rock area north of the confluence of the Columbia and Spokane Rivers, the area between the Eagle Peak and the Brody Creek faults, and near Mica Mountain west of the Sanpoil River have the Cordova group present. In the Castle Rock Creek-Mitre Rock area, greenstone layers are present throughout the exposed Covada section, and because the greenstone is resistant, it forms ridges. Clastic rocks of the Castle Rock Creek-Mitre Rock area contain granitic lithic fragments. Covada Group rocks in this area are folded; bedding strikes nearly north-south and dips steeply. Covada Group rocks exposed between the Eagle Peak and Brody Creek faults lack greenstone and limestone layers. In this area, bedding is typically planar, and there is little evidence of folding. Covada Group rocks in the Mica Mountain area consist chiefly of andalusite-bearing biotite-muscovite schist; kink folds are visible in outcrops.

Interstratified light-brown to gray conglomerate, debris flow breccia-conglomerate, pebbly volcaniclastic sandstone, tuffaceous sandstone and siltstone, and minor airfall tuff. The unit was deposited in a predominantly fluvial sedimentary environment draining a volcanic terrain, and it includes deposits from floods, mudflows, debris flows, and moderate- to low-energy stream systems. Boulder and cobble conglomerate consists of abundant well rounded dark porphyritic andesite clasts up to 2 m in diameter in a matrix of clay, typically white montmorillonite, and forms 2-3-m-thick channel fills cut into finer gravel conglomerate and sandstone. The breccia conglomerate forms single beds up to 3.5 m thick that lack internal structure, are very poorly sorted, and contain angular to subrounded boulders and cobbles in a matrix of white to buff clay and pumice fragments. The sandstones are thin bedded, well sorted, and form lensoidal deposits up to 6 m thick. Near Greenleaf Peak northwest of the Bonneville landslide, 370 m of the formation is exposed in the slide scarp. In the Vanouver area, total thickness of unit is 150 to 365 m. The Eagle Creek rests unconformably on late Oligocene volcaniclastic rocks and is unconformably overlain by middle Miocene Grande Ronde Basalt and Quaternary basalt flows.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: North Fork Camp, hybrid gneiss of
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Granitoid rocks with a wide variety of compositions and textures. The unit is an elliptical, northeast-trending body along the North Fork Toats Coulee Creek (T. 39 N., R. 24 E.) The central and western parts of the North Fork Camp hybrid gneiss are gneissic and migmatitic; the eastern part is directionless and porphyritic. Compositions range from tonalite to quartz monzonite. Principal constituents are plagioclase (oligoclase-andesine), quartz, microcline, biotite, and hornblende. Accessory minerals include epidote, chlorite, magnetite, sphene, and apatite. Microcline forms phenocrysts as much as 2 cm long in the porphyritic rocks. The North Fork Camp hybrid gneiss grades into the Tillman Mountain tonalitic gneiss, the South Fork quartz monzonite, and the Bowers quartz diorite. The North Fork Camp unit is thought to be formed by injection of the South Fork quartz monzonite and possibly the Bowers quartz diorite into zones of active cataclasis and recrystallization in the older Tillman Mountain tonalitic gneiss. Discordant K-Ar hornblende and biotite ages of 170 +/- 5 Ma and 151 +/- 5 Ma, respectively, are reported for the unit. The radiometric ages and cross-cutting relations suggest that formation of this hybrid unit occurred some time in the Early Jurassic.

Medium-grained, directionless hornblende diorite. Principal constituents are 50 to 55 percent twinned and zoned andesine (An45 with rims of An35), 30 percent hornblende, 5 to 10 percent quartz, and about 5 percent biotite. Magnetite is the most common accessory mineral; epidote and, more rarely, sphene are also present. The hornblende diorite unit forms a small, elongate stock in the Texas Creek drainage (T. 32 N., R. 22 E.). The hornblende diorite is clearly intruded by the main phase of the Texas Creek stock. It forms a gradational contact with the amphibolite of the Leecher Metamorphics in a zone about 100 m wide that is migmatitic in places. Although the actual contact is indistinct, the numerous dikes, veins, and rotated inclusions in the zone suggest an intrusive contact. The hornblende diorite is as described an older phase of the Texas Creek stock, but it is believed the unit to be distinct from the Texas Creek stock. Replicate hornblende K-Ar ages of the unit are 84.4 and 86.5 Ma, suggesting that the unit is a marginal phase of the Texas Creek stock. Because it lacks foliation and it intrudes the Leecher Metamorphics, the diorite is probably younger than the Cretaceous-Jurassic tonalite gneiss of the Okanogan complex, whose contact with the diorite is not exposed.

Vesicular, plagioclase-clinopyroxene-olivine phyric basalt and basaltic andesite intracanyon lava flows with basaltic andesite, basalt, and andesite geochemistry in the Carlton Creek-Summit Creek area.

Light-gray, abundantly phyric, augite-olivine basalt. Phenocrysts consist of randomly oriented platelets of plagioclase and granular augite and olivine, in a diktytaxitic groundmass. The basalt forms blocky jointed pahoehoe lava flows 1-7 m thick, erupted from fissures at the south end of East Crater. Erosion has partially exposed the feeder dikes. The unit has an average cumulative thickness of 37 m and an estimated volume of 4.0 cubic kilometers. The basalt of Thomas Lake is one of the oldest units of the Indian Heaven volcanic field. Accumulated volume to time models for the Indian Heaven volcanic field suggest the age should be 1.5 to 2.0 m.y., assuming a steady rate of volcanism over time.

Moderately to well-sorted conglomerate, sandstone, siltstone, shale, and clay that is locally unsorted. Bedding is massive- to well-developed and locally planar- to cross-stratified; conglomerate is commonly massive to poorly bedded. Conglomerate contains rounded to angular volcanic, plutonic, gneissic, chert, argillite, serpentinite, and quartz clasts that range in size from 1 to 7 cm, locally as large as 40 cm. Matrix is commonly coarse sand to locally silt and clay (diamict). Sandstone, commonly grading into or interbedded with conglomerate, ranges from coarse- to fine-grained (locally arkosic) and is commonly planar- or cross-bedded. Sandstone is composed predominantly of quartz, feldspar, and lithic grains in variable proportions, with local volcanic-rich interbeds. Shale and clay are commonly thinly plane-bedded and locally contain coalified debris on bedding surfaces. Shale is locally highly ferruginous. Scour features are common at the basal contacts of conglomerate beds. Sandstone and conglomerate are poorly cemented by calcite or hematite. Color is yellowish brown for ferruginous cemented rock; sandstones commonly weather buff to light-brown and are greenish- gray on unweathered surfaces; shale and clay vary from blue to yellow. Thickness ranges from very thin (less than 1 m) to possibly 500 m along western Sumas Mountain. Provenance data suggest local and distant sources of detritus. Angular discordance has been suggested between the Huntingdon and Chuckanut Formations on Sumas Mountain. The age of the Huntingdon Formation in the Bellingham area is Late Eocene to possibly Early Oligocene as determined from a single pollen analysis. Based on age and stratigraphic control in southern British Columbia, it was concluded that this unit (exposures in Washington State) is correlative with strata of the Chuckanut Formation. Outcrops are present on Sumas and Vedder Mountains. Clay from this unit has been mined for refractory purposes.

Predominantly andesite to dacite breccia forming massive cliffs, locally weakly bedded. Rocks are plagioclase phyric, but phenocrysts are highly altered and mafic minerals are replaced by chlorite. Includes some probable hypabyssal holocrystalline pyroxene andesite porphyry.

Small stocks of unknown age and composition crop out near Tamarack Peak (sec. 27, T. 38 N., R. 17 E.), on Majestic Mountain (sec. 24, T. 37 N., R. 16 E.), south of Early Winters Creek (sec. 36, T. 36 N., R. 18 E.), and near Osceola Peak (sec. 35, T. 39 N., R. 18 E.). These intrusions have been mapped only in a reconnaissance fashion and have not been described. Little is known about the age of these intrusions except that they all cut sedimentary rocks that are no older than the Harts Pass Formation.
