Two or more flows and dikes of the Roza chemical type; minor tephra; gray-black; locally includes several meters of saprolite, subarkosic sandstone, and siltstone at the base of the member where the Frenchman Springs Member is absent; fine- to medium-grained; reddish brown-weathering; discrete plagioclase phenocrysts averaging 10 mm across present almost everywhere; in places, clotted plagioclase phenocrysts; microphenocrysts of olivine and augite in an intergranular matrix; transitional to reversed magnetic polarity; average thickness about 40 m, generally increasing from east to west; well-developed colonnade with columns as much as 1 m in diameter; present along the west side of the Lewiston basin, between the Lewiston and Troy basins, and widely distributed; feeder dikes in the Grande Ronde River canyon, Asotin Creek, and in the Snake River canyon to the north of the present map area; Big Butte and Little Butte are two of the more southerly of many Roza vents; older than Priest Rapids Member (14.5 Ma) and younger than Frenchman Springs Member (15.3 Ma). The Roza Member, because of its large and persistent plagioclase phenocrysts and wide distribution, is a key marker unit across much of the Columbia Basin.  Locally, especially near vents, several thin flows may be present; flows emanated from a narrow, linear vent system evidenced by dikes and vents, tephra deposits (including welded spatter), and relict cones that trend northwest from just north of Enterprise, OR, (T. 17 N., R. 39 E.), a distance of more than 120 km; dikes present along the Snake River; prevailing slope directed flows westward; rubbly margin of a columnar Roza flow exposed on the east edge of the Snake River canyon (sec. 35, T. 13 N., R. 44 E.). The Roza Member has a higher MgO content than the Frenchman Springs Member. The Roza Member overlies the Frenchman Springs Member, but elsewhere it overlies the N2 magnetostratigraphic unit of the Grande Ronde Basalt.  The Roza Member typically consists of no more than two flows that have a total thickness of about 50 m. Where the member consists of two flows, the upper flow possesses reversed polarity, and the lower flow has transitional polarity. In the western part of the Columbia Basin, the presence of thick sedimentary interbeds between the Roza Member and the Frenchman Springs Member suggests that a significant amount of time elapsed between eruption of these two members. Therefore, the Roza Member is considered nearer in age to the overlying Priest Rapids Member (about 14.5 Ma) than to the Frenchman Springs Member. The Priest Rapids Member, the Roza Member, and the Frenchman Springs Member make up the Wanapum Basalt.

Mostly gray to black, locally reddish, porphyritic two-pyroxene andesite lava and breccia. Phenocrysts and glomerocrysts of plagioclase, clinopyroxene, hypersthene, and opaque minerals and microlites of plagioclase in devitrified groundmass. Rare brown hornblende (mostly altered to chlorite). Mostly highly altered. Massive to blocky joints. Flow layering obscure.

Fine- to medium-grained leucocratic biotite granite and granodiorite with sparse, small, equant K-feldspar phenocrysts and rounded smoky quartz grains; color index of 3 to 8. These rocks are exposed at the north end of Banks Lake. Near the contact with the migmatitic granodiorite of Gibraltar Rock, the unit contains sphene and minor, possibly xenocrystic black, elongate hornblende. The granite of Swawilla Basin is part of the Eocene-Paleocene Keller Butte pluton and the Keller Butte Suite.

Light gray, porphyritic to hypidiomorphic equigranular granodiorite; composed of anhedral, interstitial quartz and orthoclase, subhedral to euhedral plagioclase, twinned and subhedral hornblende, anhedral, ragged biotite, and anhedral magnetite; both hornblende and biotite variably altered to chlorite, fibrous amphibole (?) and Fe-Ti oxides; from 50-70 percent of the Silver Star pluton is composed of granodiorite; yielded K-Ar age of 19.6 +/- 0.7 m.y.

Massive, olive-gray to brownish-black, and porphyritic trachyandesite that consists of 1- to 3-mm-long augite and andesine phenocrysts in a microcrystalline groundmass of augite, andesine, and minor sanidine, biotite, apatite, and magnetite. The augite phenocrysts commonly form clots (glomerocrysts) in the rocks. Two small plugs of this trachyandesite crop out in the hills northeast of Oroville. The plugs cut the Oroville alkalic complex and Eocene conglomerate composed of alkalic rock clasts derived from the complex. They are compositionally similar to sills and dikes that cut Klondike Mountain Formation sedimentary rocks in the Republic area. They may be the intrusive equivalent of flows in the upper part of the Klondike Mountain Formation.

Gray, phyric, olivine basalt. Olivine phenocrysts are set in a fine-grained granular groundmass. The flows form a 122-m-high butte south of Red Mountain. The unit's informal name is derived from a hill which is locally called Alice Butte. The butte is a volcanic center, with an age stratigraphically confined to be 150,000- 500,000 years old.

Sandstone, tuffaceous sandstone, siltstone, shale, carbonaceous shale, claystone, tuff, and coal. Sandstone is feldspathic and micaceous; tabular sandstone beds are massive to crossbedded and occasionally have channel cut-and-fill structures. Light to dark siltstone forms poor outcrops, is often thinly laminated, and contains organic matter; coal beds are as thick as 16 ft. The Puget Group includes the Spiketon, Northcraft, Carbonado, Renton, Tukwila, and Tiger Mountain Formations, and additional arkosic sandstone and marine and nonmarine sedimentary rocks. Fossil leaves indicate an early Eocene to early Oligocene age for the Puget Group in the Green River area.

Interbedded, fine- to coarse-grained feldspathic-volcanic lithic (subquartzose) sandstones, conglomerate, siltstones, and silty black shales. Typical sandstones are poorly sorted and graded and contain ripple laminations and flame structures, as well as rip-up clasts of shale, all of which suggest an origin as turbidites. Sequences typical of turbidites include medium- to coarse-grained, fining-upward, poorly sorted, well-layered wackes overlain by poorly sorted, fine-grained wackes commonly exhibiting ripple and parallel laminations; the wackes are overlain by well-layered siltstone and weakly fissile silty shales that are commonly disrupted by overlying turbidites. Pebble layers are present at various intervals in the medium- to coarse-grained beds. The sandstones contain subrounded to subangular clasts of quartz, plagioclase, and volcanic rocks. The matrix consists of clay and silt-sized particles of quartz, plagioclase, opaque minerals, and white mica. The matrix and clasts are altered to calcite, sericite, pyrite, hematite, and other opaque minerals in places. Locally, the unit has been metamorphosed to prehnite-pumpellyite facies assemblages. Where intruded, the undivided Newby Group has been metamorphosed statically to hornblende-hornfels-and epidote-amphibolite-facies assemblages. In some areas, such as the Gold Creek and Buckhorn Canyon shear zones and the Smith Canyon fault zone, these rocks have been dynamothermally metamorphosed under greenschist-facies conditions and deformed in the ductile and/or brittle-ductile-transitional regimes. Rocks in these areas are foliated, lineated, and, in places, mylonitized. Quartz and calcite are present in both composite and monomineralic veins. Sandstone and argillite beds 1.5-6 m thick and containing carbonate pods are exposed south of the town of Twisp near the Alder mill. The volcanic-lithic sandstones are composed of angular volcanic fragments and plagioclase grains. The argillite is gray to black and has shaly partings. Near the Alder mill the argillite appears to be folded about steep axes.

Mostly clay, silt, and sand and minor pebbly sand deposited in a lake and interior drainage basins. Preserved shoreline features locally present. Charcoal from the unit in the Chewelah area yielded a 14C age estimate of 5,870 yr B.P.

Mostly unconsolidated dacitic ash and pumice clast deposits as thick as 3 m and sorted and crossbedded where reworked by streams. Yellow, white, and gray pumice lapilli consisting of rare crystals of green hornblende, hypersthene, plagioclase, and opaque minerals in a vesicular, clear glass matrix. The pumice is associated with a major Glacier Peak eruption 11,250 years ago.

Medium-gray, slightly phyric, olivine basalt. Flows were erupted from a vent on the south side of Sleeping Beauty and form a bench on the east side of Trout Lake Creek. The age of the unit is unknown, but is suspected to be middle Pleistocene.

Weakly consolidated, stratified sand, gravel, and cobbles of mostly sandstone and minor basalt from the Olympic Mountains core and peripheral rocks. Rare boulders greater than 1 m in diameter. Includes some peat, silt, clay, and weathered loess. Clasts are generally more rounded than clasts in till and lack facets and striations. It is poorly to moderately sorted. Weathering is gray to subtle yellow with wispy orange. The loess is commonly bioturbated, incorporating cobbles from the underlying outwash.

Light-gray to pink granite that contains equant quartz (less than ore equal to 2 mm) and K-feldspar phenocrysts in a medium- to coarse-grained (2-5 cm) groundmass composed of quartz, K-feldspar, Na-rich plagioclase (as much as 10-15 percent of rock), and biotite; magnetite is the only common accessory mineral. In some places phenocrysts make up as much as 60 percent of the rock, but elsewhere phenocrysts constitute only a few percent. The granite porphyry is exposed east of the Spokane River east of Sand Flat. Because the granite porphyry is compositionally similar to other Cretaceous plutons in the area, it is probably Cretaceous in age. Dikes of this unit cut the granodiorite of Benjamin Lake.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Keller Butte pluton, porphyritic granite of
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: A leucocratic biotite granite with K-feldspar megacrysts (less than or equal to 11 cm) in a medium- to coarse-grained, mostly equigranular groundmass. K-feldspar megacrysts typically are found in pod-like zones, and elongate quartz crystals are abundant near the margins of the unit. Plagioclase, K-feldspar, and quartz are present in nearly equal amounts; biotite makes up less than 5 percent of the rock. Accessory minerals include zircon, apatite, epidote, and magnetite. Contacts with the biotite granite of Swawilla Basin are sharp and dip steeply; neither unit is chilled. Pegmatite dikes are common in the contact zone with both the biotite granite of Swawilla Basin and the porphyritic granodiorite of Manila Creek. The quartz porphyry of Mount Tolman, porphyritic granite of Keller Butte, granite of Swawilla Basin, and porphyritic granodiorite of Manila Creek together compose the Keller Butte pluton. The quartz porphyry of Mount Tolman is the most interior phase of the Keller Butte pluton, and the porphyritic granodiorite of Manila Creek is its most exterior (border) phase. This granite has a sharp contact with granodiorite of Manila Creek. The pluton is elongate parallel to the graben structure and is cut by Sherman and Manila Pass faults. Zoned pluton with phases that form a nearly concentric pattern from the border inward: coarse-grained porphyry, medium-grained biotite granodiorite, and coarse-grained granite. The granite porphyry with quartz eyes and garnet-bearing leucocratic granite are the youngest phases.  Intrusions of the Keller Butte pluton are considered Eocene or Paleocene in age on the basis of K-Ar ages on biotite. The porphyritic granite of Keller Butte yielded ages of about 53 Ma and 61 Ma. The biotite granite of Swawilla Basin in the Nespelem area yielded an age of about 59 Ma, and, in the Coulee Dam area, an age of 53.5 Ma.

Moderately sorted to laminated with cross-bedded clay, silt, sand, and gravel to boulder terraces. Unit represents alluvium along rivers and uplifted coastal marine and estuarine deposits. Clasts of diverse compositions, ranging from iron-stained pebble gravel, gravel and local peat layers.

Mostly biotite-hornblende tonalite and granodiorite, commonly with relict clinopyroxene. Minor quartz monzodiorite and quartz diorite. Hornblende or biotite may predominate. Quartz is typically mesostasic. Color Index=8-22, but most are Color Index=12-19. Probably includes several plutons.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Blue Mountain unit of the Crescent Formation
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Gray to black lithic sandstone, semischist, siltstone, slate, granule or pebble conglomerate, and siltstone- or slate-clast breccia; commonly laminated and rhythmically bedded; local very thick sandstone beds; abundant muscovite and basalt detritus; metamorphosed to zeolite facies; foraminiferal assemblages referable to the Ulatisian or older stages.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Scotia area, leucocratic plutonic rocks of
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Mixture of muscovite-biotite quartz monzonite, alaskite, pegmatite, and aplite dikes and sills. All rock types are leucocratic and contain muscovite and sodic plagioclase (An0-30); most rocks contain at least some biotite. Alaskite and quartz monzonite are medium to coarse grained; aplite and pegmatite have textures typical of those rock types. The unit is foliated, and parts of it are sheared and have cataclastic textures. Leucocratic rocks intruded the heterogeneous metamorphic rocks. Pods of heterogeneous metamorphic rocks (less than or equal to 60 m long) are present in the leucocratic plutonic rocks, and about 5 km west of Scotia Valley the metamorphic pods may be Newman Lake Gneiss. Because abundant dikes and sills of leucocratic plutonic rocks extend into the heterogeneous metamorphic rocks, the contact between the two units is actually a transition zone. The ages of the four rock types that compose the unit are unknown. Quartz monzonite is cut by alaskite, pegmatite, and aplite. Some quartz monzonite is similar to the quartz monzonite of the Cretaceous Phillips Lake Granodiorite and may be similar in age. However, emplacement of the leucocratic rocks may have occurred over a considerable time span and thus at least some rock may be as young as Tertiary.

Light- to medium-gray, fine-grained (less than or equal to 1 mm) monzogranite with sparse, widely scattered phenocrysts. The granite has a modal composition of Q25-30:A20-35:P30-40 and contains 5-13 percent biotite, as much as 1.5 percent hornblende, and sparse magnetite and muscovite; apatite, zircon, and titanite are the most abundant accessory minerals. The granite is massive and is more resistant than the surrounding granite of the Midnite mine pluton. The granite of Blue Creek grades into granite of the Midnite mine pluton over a distance of 15-30 m; near contacts, mafic minerals are less abundant. Gradational contacts with the Midnite mine pluton and the compositional similarity to other Cretaceous plutons in the area suggest that the granite of Blue Creek is Cretaceous in age.

A very large homogeneous body of leucocratic (average color index = 5) biotite trondhjemite and granodiorite that grades from fine- to medium-grained along its western margin to medium- to coarse-grained on the north and east. Principal constituents are plagioclase (chiefly oligoclase), quartz, microcline, and biotite. Muscovite, pink garnet, apatite, zircon, hornblende, sphene, and opaques are common accessory minerals. Quartz is present as equant to lenticular gray grains and granular aggregates as much as 3 cm long that locally impart a subporphyritic texture to the rocks. Microcline crystals are white or pink and range from 1-2.5 cm long. They increase in abundance from west to east. Sparse small (1 mm) recrystallized subhedral biotite grains and biotite aggregates are typical of the margins of the pluton, while larger (2 mm) grains and aggregates are more characteristic of the interior. The trondhjemite of Doe Mountain is a northwest-trending batholith that stretches from Spanish Creek (T. 40 N., R. 20 and 21 E.) south to the Robinson Mountain area. It extends further south into the Twisp and Omak area. The interior and eastern margin of the trondhjemite of Doe Mountain is directionless to weakly foliated. Where foliation is measurable, it generally strikes north or northeast. Within 0.5 km of the contact with the trondhjemite of Lamb Butte along the western margin of the pluton, the trondhjemite of Doe Mountain is characterized by a moderate foliation, which strikes northwest. This foliation is defined by the alignment of platy biotite and lensoid quartz grains. The northeast-striking foliation in the interior of the pluton is a primary flow foliation, while the northwest-striking foliation along the western margin of the pluton is a metamorphic foliation resulting from post-crystallization ductile deformation. The contact of the trondhjemite of Doe Mountain with the trondhjemite of Lamb Butte to the west is gradational. Dikes and irregular bodies of leucocratic trondhjemite and pegmatite that resemble the trondhjemite of Doe Mountain cut the eastern margin of the trondhjemite of Lamb Butte, suggesting that the trondhjemite of Doe Mountain intrudes the trondhjemite of Lamb Butte. The trondhjemite of Doe Mountain is locally fine to medium grained (chilled) at the contact with the trondhjemite of Lamb Butte. The trondhjemite of Doe Mountain truncates layering in the gneissic trondhjemite of Tiffany Mountain to the east, suggesting that the trondhjemite of Doe Mountain intrudes the trondhjemite of Tiffany Mountain. Schlieren, spots, and irregular inclusions of heterogeneous gneissic rocks are abundant in the trondhjemite of Doe Mountain near the contact. The nature of the contact between the trondhjemite of Doe Mountain and the granodiorite gneiss complex of the Quartz Mountain area to the north is unclear. The contact between the two units is thought to be an intrusive contact. The contact along Spanish Creek is believed to be marked by a high-angle normal fault. The crystallization age of the batholith is unknown, but Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous U-Pb zircon ages have been reported from compositionally similar intrusions in the Eagle plutonic complex of southern British Columbia. Therefore, a Cretaceous or Jurassic(?) age is tentatively assigned.
Sand and gravel; deposited as strandlines along the west side of Point Roberts and overlying older glaciomarine drift.
Moderately sorted pebble conglomerate of diverse rock types, all from Columbia River drainage. Columbia River has incised 240 m below the surface of the deposit.

The volcanic rocks of Island Mountain are a heterogeneous assemblage of lava flows, tuff, volcanic breccia, and lithofeldspathic breccia and sandstone that cover approximately 15 square kilometers at Island Mountain. lnterbedded lithofeldspathic breccia and sandstone, crystal tuff, and rhyodacite and dacite flows or sills that form the basal unit of the volcanic rocks of Island Mountain; approximately 350 m thick. The breccia is massive, poorly consolidated, and crudely stratified in layers 1 to 10 m thick. It consists of subangular pebbles and cobbles in a poorly sorted matrix of sand and clay. Clasts are chiefly feldspathic sandstone, but argillite, dacite, and andesite clasts are also present. The crystal tuff and rhyodacite flows or sills that are interbedded with the breccia and sandstone are grayish white and porphyritic and contain small phenocrysts of quartz, feldspar, and biotite. The presence of both sedimentary and volcanic rock clasts in the breccia indicates that erosion and redeposition of Cretaceous sedimentary rocks accompanied Eocene volcanism near Island Mountain.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Cascade River unit, Chelan Mountains terrane, Spider Mountain Schist
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Phyllitic quartz-rich schist and calcareous mica schist (grading into impure marble), and silicic metaporphyry. Included marbles are coarsely crystalline and gray to white and contain many impurities of quartz, plagioclase, and mica. Schist, gneiss, and amphibolite of volcanic arc origin. These rocks include the Cascade River Schist and the Spider Mountain Schist. These rocks are also correlative with the Cascade River unit. The Twentyfive Mile Creek unit and parts of the migmatitic Chelan Complex may be southwestern continuations of units of the Cascade River unit. The Cascade River unit appears to have an age of about 220 Ma, based on a recent U-Pb analysis of zircons obtained from a Cascade River unit metadacite collected in the Cascade River drainage. If the leucogneiss is metamorphosed quartz keratophyre, then the protolith age for part of the sequence may be Permian. The age is compatible with the locally intrusive nature of the 220 Ma Marblemount plutonsinto the Cascade River unit, suggesting the it is Late Triassic or older. However, the zircon age is based on discordant U-Pb analyses of a single fraction; at least some (all?) of these zircons may be detrital, and thus the Permian age is speculative.

Gray, green, purple, and brown rhyolite(?) flows, hundreds of meters thick, that form a 10-km-wide belt along the east side of the Toroda Creek graben. These flows are composed of sparse phenocrysts of plagioclase and mafic minerals in an aphanitic groundmass that contains abundant plagioclase microlites. The plagioclase phenocrysts are commonly strongly sericitized, and the mafic minerals are generally replaced by some combination of chlorite, calcite, epidote, and sphene. Euhedral shapes of the altered mafic minerals suggest that most were originally pyroxene. Whole-rock geochemical data from the flows plot in the rhyolite field on the total alkali-silica (TAS) diagram. However, the presence of silica stringers and vein lets in some of these rocks indicate that silica has been introduced during alteration. Therefore, the original geochemical composition of the flows is not known with certainty. The rhyolite(?) flows unconformably overlie Klondike Mountain Formation sedimentary rocks, Sanpoil Volcanics, and older metamorphic and granitic rocks. They are conformably(?) overlain by Klondike Mountain Formation vitrophyric and microcrystalline dacite and andesite flows. The rhyolite(?) flows have yielded four K-Ar ages ranging from 47.4 +/- 1.6 Ma to 49.1 +/- 1.7 Ma. The Klondike Mountain Formation, the youngest Tertiary stratified rock unit in the Republic area, forms broad northeast-trending belts in the Republic and Toroda Creek grabens and comprises the upper part of the Eocene volcanic strata at First Thought Mountain and near Kettle Falls. The Klondike Mountain Formation consists of a wide variety of volcanic and sedimentary rocks.

Thick-bedded, strongly foliated muscovite schist interlayered with thick-bedded to massive quartzite that contains small shreds of sillimanite accompanied by rounded aggregates of tourmaline, elongate quartz grains, and small inclusions of zircon.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Cardinal Peak pluton, contact complex of
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Medium- to coarse-grained hornblendite and hornblende diorite and gabbro that range from fine-grained to coarsely pegmatitic with hornblende crystals as much as 5 cm long. The hornblendite may be digested amphibolite or hornblende schist country rock or, less likely, inclusions of the Riddle Peaks pluton. The complex is cut by dikes of the core rocks; contacts are sharp or gradational. Metamorphic host rocks typically grade into rocks of the contact complex through an increase in the amount of included igneous material; however, some contacts are sharp. Hornblendite contacts are both gradational or sharp into gabbro.

Gray, aphyric to very fine-grained, olivine basalt flows. In thin section, the texture is intergranular to diktytaxitic, with phenocrysts of plagioclase and olivine in a holocrystalline groundmass of plagioclase, clinopyroxene, olivine, and opaque minerals. The olivine phenocrysts are commonly resorbed and partially altered to iddingsite. The flows are dense and blocky to columnar jointed and have interbeds of breccia and scoria 3-5 m thick. The cumulative thickness is about 85 m. The flows form a large, isolated shield volcano south and southeast of Gilmer, capped by a scoria cone consisting of red to dark-gray, poorly sorted, unconsolidated, and stratified scoria. The basalt has a whole rock K-Ar age of 1.76 +/- 0.5 m.y.b.p. and has a reversed remanent magnetic polarity.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Mount Adams, andesite and olivine andesite flows of
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Porphyritic andesite flows and flow breccia forming the Mount Adams stratovolcano. Aphyric to slightly phyric olivine andesite flows of the main cone. Medium-gray, bluish-gray, and pinkish-gray pilotaxitic andesite forms blocky flows with platy jointing. Crude columnar jointing occurs locally in many flows, but well developed columnar jointing is restricted to the thickest flows. In thin section, phenocrysts consist of plagioclase, hypersthene, augite, and less common olivine, in a groundmass of plagioclase laths, pigeonite, magnetite, and varying amounts of glass. In many flows, glomeroporphyritic clots of the phenocrysts are common. The flows have constructed a stratovolcano 3,742 m high, standing about 3 km above its surrounding base, covers an area of 650 km2, and has a total volume of about 350 km3. The bulk of the present cone is younger than 270,000 +/- 40,000 yr b.p. The older andesitic complex, upon which the present cone is built, has been determined for a flow exposed in the Klickitat River canyon. Flows belonging to the older complex are shown separately as dacite flows. The dacite of Olallie Lake may be an early Mount Adams product. The bulk of the Mount Adams volcanism is late Pleistocene, but minor recent flows have also been mapped.

Directionless to weakly foliated tonalite. Primary constituents are plagioclase (An32 (cores), An10 (rims), biotite, quartz, and sphene. Magmatic epidote is common in all but the southernmost portion of the pluton. Hornblende and orthoclase are minor constituents. The composition is fairly uniform throughout the 120 square kilometers covered by the batholith. Well-foliated portions of the unit are mapped as the Oval Peak batholith orthogneiss. The batholith is elongate southeast and is intrusive into and in fault contact with the Twisp Valley Schist. The northeastern border of the pluton is mylonitized along the Twisp River-Foggy Dew fault zone. The southwestern contact is gradational with the Oval Peak batholith orthogneiss unit. Sphene from a weakly foliated sample of the batholith yielded a U-Pb age of 60 +/- 2 Ma. A sample from the foliated margin of the batholith yielded a similar U-Pb zircon age (61.3 +/- 2 Ma). Sphene from weakly foliated tonalite has been dated by U-Pb at 65.3 Ma. These ages record crystallization of the batholith at about 61 Ma.

Dense black microporphyritic olivine basalt; microphenocrysts of plagioclase, clinopyroxene, and olivine in intersertal groundmass of plagioclase, clinopyroxene, opaque minerals, and brown glass. Weathers red and is locally columnar jointed. Locally altered to siliceous white rock.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Huckleberry Formation, greenstone member, Windermere Group
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Light- and dark-green flows, volcanic breccias, and tuff. Individual flows and breccia units are traceable only over short distances; outcrops are massive and resistant. Where sheared, the rocks are phyllitic or schistose and have well-developed cleavage. Major- and trace-element geochemistry is consistent with that of a tholeiitic basalt extruded in a continental rift setting. Most flow rock is fine grained to aphanitic, and some is porphyritic. In some places, the relict primary texture indicates that some rock contained glass and that much of the rock was vesicular. Mafic minerals make up about 50 percent of the rock and are completely altered to chlorite, titanite, leucoxene, and tremolite. Plagioclase phenocrysts make up less than or equal to 10 percent of the porphyritic rock. Most minerals are albitized, chloritized, and (or) epidotized. Plagioclase, as phenocrysts and in the groundmass, is replaced by epidote, clay, chlorite, pumpellyite, and titanite. However, pyroxene phenocrysts are relatively unaltered. Relict primary minerals are surrounded by a haze of alteration minerals and finely disseminated opaque minerals. In many places, flow rock contains amygdules filled with calcite, chlorite, or epidote. Relict primary texture indicates that much of the volcanic rock was hyaloclastite. North of Huckleberry Creek the greenstone member includes a few meters of conglomerate at its base. Pillows are rare. The greenstone is locally schistose. The thickness of the greenstone member is varied, but the member seems to thicken from south to north. The estimated maximum thickness is 900 m thick. The greenstone member is unconformably overlain by the Monk Formation or by the Addy Quartzite. Contact with the underlying conglomerate member is a bed-by-bed gradation; the contact is placed at the base of the lowest massive flow rock. Where the conglomerate member is absent, the greenstone member unconformably overlies Middle Proterozoic rocks of the Deer Trail Group. The greenstone member is correlated with the Leola Volcanics in the Colville area. The Huckleberry Formation consists of an upper sequence of metavolcanic rocks and a lower sequence of conglomeratic rocks. In many places, the conglomeratic rocks are absent or are present only as thin layers in the lower part of the metavolcanic rock sequence. Two sequences are referred to as the greenstone member and conglomerate member of the Huckleberry Formation following the usage of Campbell and Loofbourow (1962).

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Kettle Falls, basic intrusive rock near
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Dark greenish-gray, fine- to medium-grained, equigranular diorite and gabbro composed of euhedral to subhedral plagioclase and pyroxene crystals, 1 to 2 mm long, and minor black opaque minerals. Pyroxene is generally altered to chlorite and calcite, and plagioclase is commonly altered to sericite. Whole-rock geochemical data indicate compositions ranging from basalt to andesite. These intrusive rocks are exposed in the hills north and west of Kettle Falls. The largest body, a narrow northeast-trending intrusion along the southeastern flank of Gold Hill, was apparently emplaced along a fault separating Triassic-Permian(?) metasedimentary rocks and Permian metasedimentary rocks. The smaller intrusions cut rocks as young as Triassic. These relations, and the fact that the basic intrusive rocks have not been metamorphosed, suggest that they were emplaced in the late Mesozoic or early Tertiary. An Eocene(?) age is tentatively assigned.

Aphanitic, pillowed, basaltic greenstone that forms lenses as much as 20 m thick in the southern part of the rocks near Bradeen Hill on the east side of the Columbia River. The lenses thicken along strike to the north, where they comprise as much as 30 percent of the section. These rocks are similar in composition to greenstones in the Covada Group. Dark-green-gray to medium-gray, basaltic greenstone, lapilli tuff, and schist. Greenstone contains 30 to 50 percent chlorite, 20 to 30 percent plagioclase, 10 to 15 percent iron oxide, and 5 to 15 percent calcite, and accessory zeolite, hematite, and rutile. It includes flows with pillows or calcite-filled vesicles. It is intercalated with limestone and quartzite. A lateral facies change from greenstone in the southern part of Echo Valley to green argillite and tuff in the northern part exists. The unit is generally sheared and has a sharp contact with the wacke unit on Rattlesnake Mountain. Quartz- and chert-bearing arenite and wacke, basaltic greenstone, quartz-bearing argillaceous rocks, chert-pebble conglomerate, and limestone are present in Echo Valley where they are in fault contact with lower Paleozoic rocks. Conodonts, including several species of Palmatolepis, have been identified as early Late Devonian (early Famennian) from a carbonate-barite-bearing lens east of the Uribe mine. It is suggested that the greenstone unit with minor interbedded quartzite in the Echo Valley area may correlate with a similar sequence of basaltic volcanic rocks in the Covada Group, where Ordovician macrofossils and conodonts have been recovered.

Medium- to coarse-grained tonalitic orthogneiss metamorphosed to amphibolite facies. Primary constituents are hornblende, biotite, epidote, plagioclase, and quartz. Plagioclase commonly occurs as porphyroclasts. The unit is strongly foliated and lineated and commonly protomylonitic. Foliation is defined by biotite, hornblende, and sphene. Plagioclase porphyroclasts show relict oscillatory zoning. Recrystallized plagioclase (An16 to An30) forms a fine- to medium-grained mosaic with quartz. The quartz displays deformation bands and subgrains. Rocks in this unit have a higher color index and are coarser grained than adjacent gneisses. The thickness is varied. The Tuckaway Lake gneiss intrudes the Battle Mountain gneiss, the oldest of the orthogneisses structurally underlying the Oval Peak batholith. In some places the Battle Mountain gneiss occurs as screens in the Lake Juanita leucogneiss and less commonly in the Tuckaway Lake gneiss. The Battle Mountain gneiss bears a superficial resemblance to the Reynolds Peak phase of the Black Peak batholith, and the two may be part of the same unit. They are in close proximity northeast of Battle Mountain, where the nature of the northern termination of the Battle Mountain gneiss is unclear. The Battle Mountain gneiss has not been dated. However, the unit intrudes and is deformed along the Ross Lake fault zone. The correlation of the unit's plutonic age with that of the Reynolds Peak phase of the Cretaceous Black Peak batholith is speculative. Deformation may have been latest Cretaceous, but was most likely Tertiary. Ar-Ar and K-Ar hornblende cooling ages in nearby amphibolite of the Twisp Valley Schist indicate that amphibolite facies metamorphism ended by about 55-57 Ma. The Battle Mountain gneiss appears to share the same metamorphic history as the Twisp Valley Schist, and for this reason, the Battle Mountain gneiss is assigned an age of Paleocene.

Andesitic to dacitic tuff and tuff breccia; partially to highly altered. The tuff is very poorly exposed west of Willard and south and east of Hauk Butte. The unit may be equivalent to the tuffaceous volcaniclastic rocks, which would make it upper Oligocene to lower Miocene.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Mt Rainier, andesite of, Observation and Echo Rocks andesites
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Dark-colored olivine andesite flows forming dissected remnants of two satellite cones on northwestern flank of Mount Rainier; flows from vents at Observation and Echo Rocks are as old as the Fraser glacial period (late Pleistocene).

Medium-grained hypersthene-clinopyroxene quartz monzodiorite and quartz monzonite, locally with biotite and very minor hornblende. Normatively some is granodiorite; Color Index=12-19. Euhedral biotite common near roof above Lake Ann.

Predominantly fluvial, tan or gray where weathered, zeolitic, locally carbonate-cemented, medium-grained, micaceous feldspathic to litho-feldspathic subquartzose sandstone averaging 40, 48, and 12 percent quartz, feldspar, and lithic clasts, respectively, and containing 40 to 80 percent quartz, 20 to 50 percent feldspar, and 5 to 15 percent lithics. In part contains laumontite, clinoptilolite, and prehnite. Basal beds resting on Easton Metamorphic Suite consist of pebbly sandstone containing quartz and phyllite clasts, which rapidly grade up section into more feldspathic sandstone. Thin to very thick bedded, poorly sorted, locally crossbedded with cut-and-fill structures, and with lesser interbeds of carbonaceous siltstone and shale, pebbly sandstone, and conglomerate. Pattern indicates zone of sheared rocks.

Unit is composed mainly of nongraded, 1 to 50 m thick, multistory lithic sandstones and matrix-supported granule conglomerates. These medium- to very coarse-grained rocks are laterally discontinuous and vertically separated by a few meters to more than 100 m of thin- to medium bedded sandstone, siltstone, claystone, and shale. Most exposures include five or more vertically stacked beds, ranging from 0.5-5 m thick. Except for rare, poorly developed, normally graded beds, most sandstone beds are massive. However, individual thick sandstone beds with massive bases and widely spaced, parallel laminations and (or) parallel banding developed within a meter of the top are also present. Both the massive sandstone sequences and sandstone beds with laminated/banded tops are generally lenticular on an outcrop scale, although map patterns suggest that some larger packets are tabular. Dish structures are present in some outcrops, and loading features are present on some bedding planes. Rare tool marks and current lineations generally trend northeast or southwest. A few Bouma sequences have been observed in the Kalaloch Creek basin. The sandstone and granule conglomerates are lithic to lithofeldspathic arenites. They are medium- to very coarse-grained and moderately to well-sorted. Most massive or laminated/ banded sandstone beds contain rip-up clasts or intraclasts of mudstone, very dark-gray siltstone, and (or) tuffaceous siltstone. These clasts are generally tabular, range from 0.3 mm to more than 30 cm in length, and are oriented parallel to bedding. Many of the tabular rip-up clasts taper to very thin, fragile edges. They are gray, dark gray, or olive gray and weather tan or light gray. The massive to thick-bedded sandstones in unit were mostly deposited from sandy debris flows in a bathyal open-marine environment. Thin-bedded rocks within unit are mostly interpreted as deep-marine interdistributary and levee deposits. Minor siltstone-, shale-, and slate-clast breccia, and pebble conglomerate. Common platy shale, slate, or siltstone clasts. Consists of part of the Hoh rock assemblage.

Greenschist, dark-gray to black, pyritic argillite and chert, wacke, limestone, and conglomerate interbedded with minor green-gray, fine-grained porphyritic flows and flow breccia; includes conglomerate interbedded with flows along Flat Creek.

The volcanic rocks of Island Mountain are a heterogeneous assemblage of lava flows, tuff, volcanic breccia, and lithofeldspathic breccia and sandstone that cover approximately 15 square kilometers at Island Mountain (T. 39 N., R. 19 E.). Gray, aphyric to weakly porphyritic andesite flows and flow breccias that form the upper 200 m of the volcanic rocks of Island Mountain. The andesite is composed of less than 5 percent phenocrysts of plagioclase, hornblende, and clinopyroxene in an aphanitic groundmass. The rocks are commonly altered; secondary minerals include sericite, albite, calcite, magnetite, and chlorite. Thin crystal lithic tuff beds are locally intercalated with the flows and flow breccias.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Pysht Formation, upper Twin River Group, sandstone of
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Massive and thin-bedded, poorly indurated, olive-gray sandy siltstone and mudstone; mollusk bearing and concretionary with beds of fine- to medium-grained, thin-bedded, subfeldspathic sandstone; highly susceptible to landsliding. Foraminiferal assemblages are assigned to lower part of the Saucesian and upper part of the Zemorrian Stages; mollusks are indicative of the Juanian Stage.

Youngest outburst flood deposits from ice dams along the Columbia River; consists mainly of reworked Qfg3. Gravels; grain size ranges from sand to boulders, size generally decreases away from major Pleistocene outburst flood channels; clasts chiefly basalt in abandoned flood channels in northeastern map area; clasts chiefly basalt, granite, quartzite, diorite, and volcanic porphyries along the Columbia and Snake Rivers; generally matrix-poor, and where matrix is present, it is composed of basalt, quartz, and feldspar sand to granule grains; divided into four units on the basis of magnetic polarity, presence of ash beds, pedogenic carbonate development, and stratigraphic position; deposited by outburst floods from glacial Lake Missoula and other ice-margin lakes; displays numerous bedding forms including massive, large-scale cross-bedded and plane-bedded channel and bar deposits; same age as outburst flood deposits, silt and sand.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Bare Mountain, basaltic andesite and basalt flows of
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Light- to medium-gray olivine-pyroxene-phyric basaltic-andesite to basalt forming multiple, thick, blocky-jointed lava flows; maximum thickness 83 m; unit has largest present volume of any Quaternary flow in the Soda Peaks-West Crater area; age estimated between 10,000 to 20,000 yr.

Dark-gray, phyric, olivine basalt. Basalt forms fine-grained, dense to diktytaxitic, blocky jointed flows 3-35 m thick and a lava cone north-northwest of the town of White Salmon. The basalt flowed to the west, reaching the White Salmon River. The age is unknown, but the unit may be related to the basalt of White Salmon and the Underwood volcano, about 850,000 years old.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: eastern melange belt, rocks of the
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Gray to white, lenticular beds and pods of banded medium- to fine-grained crystalline marble intercalated with metachert and greenstone, locally with chlorite; coarsely crystalline. In part, shaley laminations or graphitic impurities mark bedding planes. Silicified replacement masses. The deposits south of White Horse are mostly in small pods.

Continental sedimentary rocks consisting of an upper member of clayey fluvial sand and gravel derived from volcanic rock, with thin silt and clay lenses and wood fragments, and a lower member of lacustrine and fluvial quartzose sand and kaolinitic clay. The formation is cohesive and compact. Maximum known thickness is about 100 ft; the upper member is about 75 ft thick and the lower member about 28 ft thick. The lower member includes volcanic ash beds and woody lignite. Hammer Bluff Formation crops out along the north channel wall of the Green River southwest of Black Diamond and is bounded by angular unconformities both above and below. It is overlain by Orting Drift and underlain by rocks of the Puget Group. An assemblage of fossil plants near the bottom of the upper member is late Miocene. The upper member is strongly iron stained, includes many stones and sand grains partly weathered to clay, and is relatively clay-rich and impermeable, causing slope failure.

Generally coarse-grained, hornblende-plagioclase gabbro to diorite with minor pyrrhotite, olivine, and quartz in sill-like bodies, from 3 m to more than 100 m thick, that intrude the Prichard Formation in the southeastern corner of the map. Some of the thicker sills are zoned. Sills are generally present more than 1,200 m below the contact with the Burke Formation; the number and thickness of the sills increases down-section. The Crossport C Sill is approximately 2,300 m below the Burke-Prichard contact.

Phyllite and quartzite intercalated with thin, discontinuous lenses of chert-pebble metaconglomerate, metalimestone, and greenstone. These rocks form a northwest-trending belt along the West Fork Sanpoil River in the Oroville and Republic area. No fossils have been recovered from these metasedimentary rocks, but believed to be correlative with the Anarchist Group because they contain chert-pebble metaconglomerate and blue quartzite, which are distinctive lithologies in the Anarchist Group. Greenschist-facies metasedimentary rocks are believed to grade into amphibolite-facies metamorphic rocks that are probably thermally upgraded Anarchist Group metasediments. However, the contact between the greenschist-facies and amphibolite-facies rocks is abrupt and probably marked by a fault. The amphibolite-facies rocks is believed to be part of the Okanogan metamorphic core complex. The Anarchist Group consists of two formations, the Spectacle and Bullfrog Mountain Formations. Phyllite, slate, metawacke, and chert-pebble metaconglomerate are the principal constituents of both formations. The Spectacle Formation also contains metalimestone and minor greenstone. Permian brachiopods, pelecypods, gastropods, corals, and crinoid columnals have been recovered from the Spectacle Formation. The Anarchist Group is correlative with the Cache Creek Group in southern British Columbia. The Anarchist Group is thought to unconformably be overlain by the Kobau Formation and Palmer Mountain Greenstone. The Anarchist Group is separated from those units by a regional thrust fault.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: western melange belt, rocks of the
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Serpentinized peridotite, pyroxenite, and dunite. Nearby Tertiary plutons have recrystallized ultramafic rocks to higher grade assemblages, locally with enstatite and talc. Pyroxenite is predominantly coarse-grained anhedral and fine-grained subhedral to euhedral clinopyroxene in a sea of serpentine minerals with mesh structure.

Medium-grained, pink to white leucocratic granodiorite with biotite books (0.5-1.0 cm) and honey-brown sphene. The stock contains xenoliths (5-10 cm) of amphibolite interlayered with granoblastic plagioclase and poikilitically enclosed quartz. Mafic xenoliths of amphibolite with aligned hornblende are considered to be part of the Leecher Metamorphics.  The Noname stock crosscuts foliation in the Methow Gneiss. The stock, which is fairly unaltered, is elongate east-west and covers less than 8 square kilometers. It passively intruded the Methow Gneiss, forming a 10-m-wide contact zone which crosscuts foliation in the gneiss. It has also been called the Methow stock and the French Creek stock. The stock crops out at the town of Methow on both sides of the Methow River.

Lenses and angular blocks of sandstone, siltstone, shale, conglomerate, and volcanogenic rocks in a matrix of either black shale with scaly cleavage or intensely sheared sandstone and siltstone; includes diapiric muds, fault breccias, and submarine landslide deposits; includes part of the Hoh rock assemblage. Unit consists of thick sequences of intensely sheared marine sedimentary and minor basaltic volcanogenic rocks; volcanogenic rocks are tectonic blocks, range from granules to boulders, and have abundant chlorite and epidote; interpreted as unusually wide fault gouge zones. In the sheared sedimentary rocks, the cleavage is oriented subparallel with the lithologic layering and wraps around sandstone phacoids. Sandstones within unit range from granules to boulders several tens of meters across, and are lithofeldspathic arenites, but randomly oriented bedding indicates that these are either exotic blocks or rotated phacoids. In the Forks area, also includes melanges injected along fault planes or as piercement structures, and coastal areas where sea stacks of randomly varying lithology and metamorphic grade lie in close proximity (and apparent disequilibrium) with each other. The matrix of unit melanges consists of very dark clay and lesser amounts of sheared admixtures of thin-bedded sandstone, siltstone, and shale and volcanogenic rocks. The clay is silty and commonly. The clay has a distinctive, penetrative, scaley cleavage that is parallel with the faults that bound these units or forms a concentric pattern in map view.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: western melange belt, rocks of the
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Massive to foliated, fine- to medium-grained metagabbro and metadiorite. Outcrops sheared on all scales. In massive rocks, euhedral, mottled, locally crushed plagioclase, intergranular to euhedral uralitized clinopyroxene and opaque minerals are common. Metamorphic minerals are albite(?), uralite, chlorite, sphene, and carbonate minerals.

Light- to medium-gray to black, fine- to coarse-grained, thickly laminated to massive limestone, marble, and siliceous marble in pods and beds interbedded with elastic rocks and greenstone. Accessory minerals include subangular quartz grains, chlorite, sericite, plagioclase, and carbonaceous material. Lenses range in thickness from 2 m to 60 m. Late Devonian conodonts from a 5-m-thick bed of gray, fine-grained, barite-bearing limestone intercalated with siliceous argillite 50 m east of the Uribe mine have been identified. Fossils include eight species of Palmatolepis, Polygnathus sp., and Priunrodina cf. Pr. alternata. Studies of this collection and concluded that it represents the palmatolepid biofacies of the lower part of the early Famennian Upper crepida Zone. Quartz- and chert-bearing arenite and wacke, basaltic greenstone, quartz-bearing argillaceous rocks, chert-pebble conglomerate, and limestone are present in Echo Valley where they are in fault contact with lower Paleozoic rocks. Conodonts, including several species of Palmatolepis, were identified as early Late Devonian (early Famennian) from a carbonate-barite-bearing lens east of the Uribe mine.  lnterbedded light- to dark-gray, thin- to medium-bedded, medium to thick graded laminated limestone, argillaceous limestone, phyllite, and chert; present north of Hunters Creek. The unit is believed to be fault-bounded and exhibits strong cleavage. A Middle Cambrian to Early Ordovician (no younger than lower Fauna C) age was assigned based on the occurrence of the conodont Furnishina sp. indet. from the outcrop on the Springdale-Hunters Road (SE1/4SE1/4NW1/4 sec. 2, T. 30 N., R. 37 E.). The conodonts have a CAI of 5, indicating that the host rock reached at least 300 degrees C. On the basis of the fossil data, the rock could be slightly older than suggested; however, the conodont samples are within a sequence of proximal turbidites, and therefore the conodonts may not be indigenous to the rock.

A melange divided into tonalite, sandstone and argillite, and greenstone of the Lopez Terrane of Whetten and Others (1978) units. Early Cretaceous (Valanginian) Buchia, Jurassic radiolarians, and a Late Jurassic or Early Cretaceous belemnite have been found in this melange. This unit is the sandstone and argillite, composed of foliated graywacke-argillite flysch with minor chert, greenstone, and conglomerate. It is highly deformed and locally tectonically mixed with the greenstone unit.

Light- to medium-gray, phyric, olivine-pyroxene basalt. The flow(s) erupted from a vent near the top of The Loaf and flowed to the southwest. The total thickness is greater than 100 m. The age of the unit is not known.

Sand and gravel; semiconsolidated fanglomerate of primarily basalt clasts cemented by iron-stained clay; surface commonly dissected and capped by a well-developed caliche layer; age inferred from geomorphology, cementing, and caliche development.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Wilbur Creek and Umatilla Members, Saddle Mountain Basalt
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Three fine-grained to very fine-grained, dense, dark-gray, aphyric to sparsely plagioclase-phyric flow lacking obvious olivine in hand sample; blocky jointing; very strongly normal magnetic polarity; present in most of the Lewiston basin but crops out poorly in most places; consists of basalts of Sillusi and Umatilla, and the Bear Creek flow of Ross (1978, 1989). Puffer Butte is a vent for the Sillusi flow; feeder dike exposed from the Grande Ronde River canyon to Puffer Butte; older than Asotin Member (13 Ma) and younger than Priest Rapids Member (14.5 Ma).

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Beckler Peak stocks, Mount Stuart batholith
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Biotite granodiorite, hypidiomorphic granular to xenomorphic with microcline microperthite. Mostly CI 5-9, but some rocks reported with as much as 18 percent mafic minerals. Stocks are commonly highly sheared and cataclastic.

Alpine outwash sand and gravel with minor interbedded silt and clay; stained reddish to yellowish brown; completely weathered to clay near the surface and moderately weathered at depth; contains volcanic rocks of the Northcraft Formation and reworked material from other adjacent Tertiary rocks; mantled with 2.0 to 4.0 m of silt and clay in many exposures.

Unsorted mixture of subangular to subrounded boulders in a matrix of sand, silt, and clay, derived from Mount Adams. The boulders, up to 20 m in diameter, become finer upward and are primarily andesite from Mount Adams with lesser olivine basalt. The mudflow originated on the southwestern flank of Mount Adams at the head of the White Salmon Glacier and flowed down the White Salmon River valley for 40 km.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: St Regis Formation, Ravalli Group, Belt Supergroup
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Interbedded siltite and argillite and subordinate quartzite. The formation is characterized by dark-red to maroon-tinted strata overlain by a distinctive zone of green-tinted strata. Finer-grained rocks are more deeply pigmented. In some places the rocks are bleached. The upper part of the formation consists of carbonate-bearing and carbonate-free, yellow-green to light-green siliceous argillite; in some places green-tinted siltite is present. Locally white, green, or gray, thin- to medium-bedded siltite and thinly laminated argillite, with minor medium- to thick-bedded quartzite are present. Most rocks in the upper part of the formation are thinly bedded to laminated. Bedding is uneven in the uppermost part of the formation. Mud-chip breccia, mud cracks, ripple marks, and cross-lamination are abundant, especially near top of the formation. Bedding ranges from thin laminations to about 1 m thick but averages about 5 cm thick. Siltite and quartzite form thicker beds, and most are capped by argillite partings. The rock unit typically displays flaggy weathering. The upper green-tinted sequence grades into rocks of the overlying Wallace Formation. The St. Regis Formation grades downward into quartzite of the Revett Formation. The lower contact is placed at the base of the horizon where siltite and argillite are more abundant than quartzite. The St. Regis Formation is about 300 to 500 m thick.

A melange consisting predominantly of greenstone and medium-grained, light-blue-gray sandstone, with minor amounts of black to brown, fine-grained sandstone, siltstone, argillite, and generally very thin bedded, black to gray chert. Locally, poorly to moderately sorted volcaniclastic sandstone, cherty sandstone, mudstone, and conglomerate with lesser ribbon chert, green tuff, and basalt and dacite pillow lava and rare limestone. Metamorphosed sandstone, argillite, mudstone, and conglomerate; commonly dark gray-brown and highly penetrated by veinlets of secondary minerals.  Clastic lithologies are commonly massive and locally graded at a scale of a few millimeters to a few centimeters; local cataclastic deformation is especially apparent toward the base of the section where many underlying lithologies are tectonically interleaved within the Constitution Formation. Sandstone is commonly turbiditic and largely contains volcanic detritus with lesser chert, nonvolcanic quartz, and epidote grains; mudstone is commonly massive and consists mainly of clay and silt sized grains with minor sand-sized grains and local olistolithic limestone and metavolcanic boulders 1-2 m in diameter. Conglomerate contains rounded to angular volcanic, chert, metaplutonic, and schistose clasts in siltstone matrix. Clasts are thought to be derived from underlying Orcas Chert, Turtleback Complex, and Garrison Schist. Clasts average 5 cm in diameter. Ribbon chert, rhythmically bedded every 3-4 cm, is interbedded with clastic rocks throughout the entire section but is more abundant near the base. Green tuff is present near the base of the section and is commonly fine-grained and indurated; intercalated mudstone and chert in tuff give it a layered appearance. Pillow lava ranges in composition from ocean-floor basalt to possibly arc-derived dacite and is interlayered with clastic rocks. Whether the pillow lava is olistolithic blocks, in place, or both is unclear. Limestone is present near the base of the unit as isolated pods. Metamorphic minerals in clastic rocks include albite + quartz + chlorite + calcite/aragonite + white mica +/- lawsonite +/- prehnite. Clastic rock is generally tan to gray on weathered surfaces and gray to dark gray on fresh surfaces, pillow lavas range from light to dark green and locally red-green, tuff is light green, chert is grayish green to pale black, and limestone is light gray. Constitution Formation of Vance (1975) may locally include units of the Turtleback Complex of McLellan (1927), Orcas Chert of Vance (1975), and Vedder Complex of Armstrong and others (1983). The age of the Constitution Formation of Vance (1975) is poorly constrained, but radiolarians from chert give Late Jurassic or Early Cretaceous ages. Structurally overlies the Orcas Formation. Outcrops are present on Orcas, Shaw, and San Juan Islands. The type locality is Mount Constitution on Orcas Island.

Dolomite, quartzite, greenstone, metalimestone, and argillite. These rocks are subdivided into two informal map units. The lower member is composed of light-gray to light-brown metadolomite with minor interlayers of quartzite, greenstone, metalimestone, and argillite. The rocks are cut by stringers and blebs of white quartz. The upper member  consists of varied amounts of fine-grained quartzite, greenstone, metalimestone, and phyllitic argillite. The unit disconformably underlies the Addy Quartzite on Mingo Mountain. The Monk Formation and Addy Quartzite on Mingo Mountain are folded into a series of doubly plunging anticlines and synclines that are structurally discordant with surrounding rock units to the west, north, and east. This structural discontinuity has been interpreted as a thrust fault. Assignment of these rocks to the Monk Formation is tentative, for it is not certain how these rocks are to be correlated with others in northern Washington, Idaho, and British Columbia. The presence of greenstone is reminiscent of the Precambrian Huckleberry Greenstone or Leola Volcanics. However, unlike the Huckleberry/Leola, the greenstone in the Kettle Falls area is not underlain by conglomerate but by rocks very much like those described as the Monk Formation. Although greenstone is not typically part of the Monk Formation in Washington and Idaho, the various rock units beneath the Cambrian quartzite in the Kettle Falls map area are considered to be Precambrian and to belong to the Monk Formation.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Blue Mountain unit of the Crescent Formation, conglomerate of
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Gray to black lithic sandstone, semischist, siltstone, slate, granule or pebble conglomerate, and siltstone- or slate-clast breccia; very dark gray to purple-gray; commonly laminated and rhythmically bedded; local very thick sandstone beds; abundant muscovite and basalt detritus. Foraminiferal assemblages referable to the Ulatisian or older stages.  Thick-bedded to massive conglomerate and pebbly sandstone or semischist with minor interbedded slate or argillite; subrounded pebbles and minor cobbles of dark-gray chert and volcanic rocks with less-abundant light-gray sandstone; very dark gray to grayish-black angular siltstone rip-up clasts common and locally form slate-chip breccia; interbedded with rocks of Eocene to Paleocene age; believed to be a submarine channel facies.

Fine- to coarse-grained feldspathic to lithofeldspathic subquartzose sandstone with interbedded siltstone, claystone, and coal. The fluvial to nearshore marine rocks attain at least 670 m thickness near Taylor Mountain. Contains 30 to 45 percent quartz, 40 to 50 percent feldspar, and 10 to 20 percent lithic grains. Micaceous feldspathic subquartzose sandstone, siltstone, claystone, and coal. Rocks in the Green River area are white, very fine grained to gritty sandstone with subangular to rounded grains consisting of about 40 to 60 percent quartz, 30 to 50 percent feldspar, and about 5 percent lithic clasts.). Tabular beds of sandstone are massive to cross bedded and occasionally exhibit channel cut-and-fill structures. Light to dark siltstones form poor outcrops, are commonly thinly laminated, and contain organic matter. Coal beds are as thick as 5 m. Near Tiger Mountain, unit consists of interbedded nonmarine sandstone and volcanic breccia belonging to undivided Tiger Mountain and Tukwila Formations.

Fine- to medium-grained tonalitic to granodioritic biotite orthogneiss. The Stehekin orthogneiss is in gradational contact with both the Purple Creek orthogneiss to the northeast and the Rainbow Mountain orthogneiss to the northwest. It is distinguished from these by its lack of hornblende and titanite. A northeast-plunging, subhorizontal stretching lineation is generally better developed than foliation. North-northeast-striking foliation is poorly to moderately developed throughout the unit. Bodies of flecked gneiss of Adams (1961) occur within the Stehekin orthogneiss. An Eocene age (about 50 Ma. above) combined with northeast-directed ductile fabrics (shallow lineation and moderate to steep foliations) suggest northeast-directed shear possibly related to Eocene ductile deformation in the Gabriel Peak Tectonic Belt to the east and (or) an extension of ductile deformation suggested by Haugerud and others (1991) to the west.  All these units are assigned a Late Cretaceous to Tertiary age based on the dating of orthogneiss bodies elsewhere in the Skagit Gneiss.

Light-tan, porphyritic hornblende dacite stocks and domes at Hauk Butte, north of Augsburger Mountain (Little Wind River plug), and north of Wind Mountain. At Hauk Butte, the dacite is fine-grained, porphyritic, grading to diorite porphyry with subhedral granular texture. The plagioclase is zoned, and the green hornblende is well preserved. The Little Wind River plug is petrographically and chemically similar to the dacite at Hauk Butte, but generally finer-grained, and is probably the result of the same intrusive/volcanic event. North of Wind Mountain, a hornblende dacite which in hand specimen appears similar to Hauk Butte rocks, had zoned plagioclase and hornblende phenocrysts in a groundmass of plagioclase laths with quartz and orthoclase. All three dacite porphyries may be related to the Wind Mountain and Shell Rock quartz diorites, also of late Miocene to Pliocene age.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Cayuse Mountain-Mill Canyon area, metasediments of
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Dark-gray, light-brown, and purple quartzite composed of quartz and as much as 25 percent unoriented, interstitial muscovite and biotite. The abundance of interstitial mica varies considerably from bed to bed, but biotite typically exceeds muscovite. Beds range from about 0.5 cm to about 0.6 m thick; cross-bedding is locally present. About 90 m of this fine- to medium-grained, impure quartzite is exposed about 3 km west of Cayuse Mountain. Neither the upper or lower contact of the quartzite is exposed and thus, the relation with the other metasedimentary rock units in the Cayuse Mountain area is unknown. Thermally upgraded rocks consisting predominantly of hornfels, phyllite, and marble, as well as subordinate quartzite and tactite. On Cayuse Mountain the rocks consist of a sequence of marble and phyllite overlying a sequence of hornfels; because the sequence overlying the hornfels is poorly exposed east of Mill Canyon, the phyllite and marble are undivided in that area. Quartzite exposed west of Cayuse Mountain is included as part of this sequence. The resemblance of parts of the Cayuse Mountain-Mill Canyon sequence to the Lower Cambrian-Upper Proterozoic Addy Quartzite and to the Ordovician-Cambrian Metaline Formation suggests that these rocks may be Ordovician to Cambrian in age, but on the basis of the unit's possible gradational contact with the probable Middle Proterozoic quartzite exposed east of the Coulee Dam area, these rocks may be Middle Proterozoic in age. Additionally, parts of the sequence resemble parts of the Ordovician Covada Group exposed in the Fort Spokane area, so these rocks may be correlative with the Covada Group. However, because the Cayuse Mountain-Mill Canyon rocks lack fossils and their contact relations and structural position are uncertain, the absolute age of the sequence is unknown.

Medium- to coarse-grained biotite ?granodiorite that contains sparse muscovite. Felsic minerals are surrounded by thin rims of very fine-grained feldspar, quartz, and mica, suggesting the rock has been quenched. Quartz veins are ubiquitous, and pyrite is commonly present, regardless of whether the rock is altered. The pluton was originally mapped as part of the Galena Point Granodiorite but was later identified as part of the granodiorite of Hall Mountain. This pluton and several other noncontiguous plutons exposed north of the Colville area constitute the granodiorite of Hall Mountain. Based on a K-Ar biotite age of 99 Ma from rock in the Colville area, the granodiorite of Hall Mountain is considered Cretaceous.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Pysht Formation, upper Twin River Group
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Massive and thin-bedded, poorly indurated, olive-gray sandy siltstone and mudstone; mollusk bearing and concretionary with beds of fine- to medium-grained, thin- to very thick-bedded, subfeldspathic, calcareous sandstone; highly susceptible to landsliding. Unweathered mudstone, claystone, and siltstone are medium gray to dark greenish gray, pale yellowish brown where weathered. Mudstone locally contains thin beds of calcareous claystone; argillaceous rocks commonly contain sparsely disseminated calcareous concretions that are spherical, cylindrical, or irregular in shape. Mollusk shell fragments, foraminifera, and carbonized plant material are common in mudstone. Foraminiferal assemblages are assigned to lower part of the Saucesian and upper part of the Zemorrian Stages; mollusks are indicative of the Juanian Stage.

Dark-gray olivine basalt or basaltic-andesite lava flow. Phenocrysts of olivine and rare augite are in a groundmass of plagioclase, clinopyroxene, olivine, magnetite, and glass. The basalt forms an intracanyon flow in the upper Rock Creek drainage. It erupted from a vent on Mowich Butte.

Porphyritic pyroxene basaltic-andesite lava flows and flow breccia with thin interbeds of red-brown siltstone, sandstone, conglomerate, and tuff; also contains lesser olivine basalt, pyroxene andesite, and platy to irregularly jointed dacite; flows are typically thin (1-4 m) and lenticular or lozenge-shaped, with wavy top and bottom contacts; thin (5-50 cm) siltstone or sandstone layers often separate flows; dense flow centers typically blocky jointed to platy; well-developed columnar-jointing or colonnade-entablature sets rare; locally, scoriaceous flow breccia forms bulk of unit, enveloping small, lenticular dense flow centers in block rubble; vugs and fractures contain characteristic assemblage of calcite and complex suite of zeolite minerals; total unit thickness exceeds 1500 m in the type area between Woodland, Washington and Kelso. In thin section, the unit is most commonly plagioclase-augite phyric with trachytic groundmass of plagioclase microlites, clinopyroxene, opaque minerals, and murky, green to brown, microcrystalline mixtures of zeolite minerals, chlorite, and volcanic glass; olivine phenocrysts also present in a few flows.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Gypsy Quartzite, purple quartzite unit of
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Purple, light-blue, white to light-gray, medium- to coarse-grained, thin- to thick-bedded quartzite. The unit is approximately 600 to 690 m thick. It displays purple to red liesegang bands which are parallel, subparallel, and transverse to bedding. Liesegang bands, hematitic cements, and heavy-mineral laminae define banding that is most prominent in the lower 400 to 450 m. The upper 200 to 300 m consist of medium- to thick-bedded, blue and purple, medium-grained to granular quartzite with planar cross-beds. Scolithus linearis burrows are present in the upper part. The base of unit is placed at the bottom of the lowest purple and blue quartzite. Light-gray and purplish, thick-bedded quartzite interbedded with gray, tan, green, and purplish argillite and siltite. The unit is 30 percent thinner on the west side of the Flume Creek fault. The lower 1,000 to 1,300 m of the Gypsy are dominated by quartzite containing minor interbedded argillite and siltite; the upper 350 to 450 m comprise an interbedded sequence of quartzite, siltite, and argillite. The position of the contact between the Maitlen Phyllite and the Gypsy Quartzite has not been consistently mapped.  The Precambrian-Cambrian boundary is present in the Gypsy Quartzite, somewhere below the first occurrence of trilobite fragments. Unfossiliferous rocks, for which a sedimentary environment similar to that for the trilobite-bearing sediments is indicated, are Precambrian in age and were deposited before the first appearance of the fauna. The Gypsy Quartzite is correlated with the Addy Quartzite of Weaver (1920). The Gypsy Quartzite may be slightly older than the Addy Quartzite because a Lower Cambrian fauna first occurs slightly higher in the section in the Gypsy. The formation is present in the cores of regional anticlines. It was deposited on a passive margin in a rapidly subsiding basin formed by rifting of the North American continent in the late Precambrian to Early Cambrian. The Gypsy Quartzite has been divided into five informal units east of the Pend Oreille River. West of the Flume Creek fault the thickness of the Gypsy Quartzite is about 30 percent less.

Micaceous feldspathic sandstone, siltstone, and very minor amount of pebble conglomerate and dark mudstone. The unit includes laharic breccia, volcaniclastic sandstone, felsite- and pumice-pebble conglomerate, fluvial conglomerate, and air-fall tuff. Clasts of the conglomerate are predominantly basaltic and andesitic, but include dacitic lavas, as well as quartzite and other metamorphic clasts. Pumiceous material is predominantly dacitic. The sandy matrix of the volcaniclastic conglomerates is mostly nonmicaceous. Fluvial and volcaniclastic deposits are weakly to moderately indurated. Interbedded with Grande Ronde and, locally, Wanapum Basalt. Deposits are composed of detritus eroded from rocks older than the Columbia River Basalt Group.  The Ellensburg Formation probably represents deposits of the ancestral Columbia River systems, especially deposits of the tributary streams draining the late Miocene Cascade Mountains. Also derived from volcanic centers in the Cascades.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Quartz Mountain stock, eastern melange belt
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Medium-grained hornblende metatonalite and metagranodiorite, locally with biotite and garnet. Hypidiomorphic granular, but with local bent plagioclase and statically recrystallized plagioclase, crystalloblastic growth of sodic plagioclase rims on K-felsdpar and plagioclase, replacement of feldspar cores by clinozoisite, and recrystallization of biotite. Stock and many its many apotheses intruded Lookout Mountain Formation of Stout (1964) with sharp contacts.

Heterogeneous hornblende tonalite, biotite tonalite and tonalite gneiss, mixed with mafic to feldspathic amphibolite, gneissic amphibolite, blastoporphyritic feldspar gneiss, migmatitic leucocratic tonalite gneiss, migmatitic mesocratic and melanocratic tonalite gneiss, migmatitic banded tonalite gneiss, and mixed to brecciated igneous and high-grade metamorphic rocks. Migmatite grades from gneissic to massive tonalite commonly rich in mafic schlieren preserved as strongly migmatitic amphibolite, gneiss, and schist. Microdiorite, a fine-grained granoblastic to xenomorphic hornblende, biotite, and plagioclase rock, is an important constituent and forms dikes and irregular bodies gradational to amphibolite. The migmatite is criss-crossed by small light-colored tonalitic to alaskitic dikes, sills, and irregular bodies, mostly with sharp contacts. Less common rocks in the migmatite are hornblende schist, biotite schist, and marble.  Two generations of migmatization are evident in some areas. U-Pb zircon and sphene ages obtained range from 82 to 113 Ma from part of the migmatite.

Thin- to thick-bedded, graded, lithic, feldspathic sandstone and lithic quartzose sandstone with lenses of pebble and cobble conglomerate and mudflow breccia; sandstone is laminated to cross-stratified; conglomerate clasts commonly are volcanic-lithic sandstone but also include reworked calcareous concretions, diabase, basalt, felsic volcanic rocks, micaceous feldspathic sandstone, chert, phyllite, and fragments of wood and mollusks. Sparse foraminifera are assigned to the Narizian Stage.

Undifferentiated yellowish brown to brown and brownish gray stony till, moraines, and boulder gravel outwash deposits from alpine glaciation. Till is weathered to a depth of about 2 m; 15 to 30 m thick. Stones near top of the till have weathering rinds which range in thickness from 0.5 to 2.5 mm; original topography considerably modified but many large moraines still recognizable; age older than 38,000 yr b.p.

Mostly massive to poorly bedded dolomite typically recrystallized to dolomitic marble, calcsilicate hornfels, tactile, and calcareous dolomitic marble. Cream-white, light-gray, blue-gray, greenish gray, tan, or red, and black, medium- to thick-bedded, fine- to coarse-grained dolomite with minor quartz. Some rock is schistose. Tremolite, titanite(?), and silica veinlets can be found in some exposures. The dolomite is locally silicified. The dolomite is interbedded with intraformational breccia, which includes the Josephine unit, siliceous dolomite, limestone, black dolomite, and massive gray, fine- to medium-grained dolomite with no apparent bedding features. The unit also includes recrystallized and siliceous dolomite associated with lead and zinc deposits in the Metaline Mining District. Bedding is poorly developed; rare desiccation cracks and gypsum or gypsum psuedomorphs can be found in the upper part (associated with mineral deposits). Where it is adjacent to plutonic rocks, the dolomite is clean, white, coarse-grained, dolomitic marble and calc-silicate rock. Locally, bedding is marked by light- and dark-gray bands 1-20 m thick. In some places dolomite contains dark shale, oncolite, and pisolite interbeds. West of Dunn Mountain, the dolomite contains chert nodules and stringers. Some of the marble has closely spaced light and dark bands similar to the zebra rock. The unit has a maximum estimated thickness of 1,500-1,800 m.  The intraformational breccia consists of dolomite fragments in a fine-grained, dark-gray, dolomite matrix which alternates in 8- to 100-m-thick sections with dark- to light-gray, medium- to fine-grained, thin-bedded dolomite. Breccia fragments are thin, subangular to angular, 1-cm- to 1.5-m long slabs broken parallel to bedding. Some clasts are preferentially oriented; they are commonly rotated. The breccia has a gradational contact with the bedded dolomite. The Josephine unit is a complex assemblage of irregularly interlayered and massive, laminated elastic rock to breccia which includes clasts of black and dark-gray, variously silicified and weakly to intensely pyritic dolomite, dolomitic breccia, limestone, argillite, and quartzite. Some fragments have distinct angular margins or are highly irregular and wispy, and have indistinct borders that appear to grade into the dolomite matrix. Fragment size ranges from sand size to 3-m-wide blocks. This unit is present below the Ledbetter contact, and it laterally interfingers with the gray limestone and bedded dolomite units. Interpretations of the origin of the breccia units include a fault breccia, solution collapse, and debris flow and slump deposits. Where possible, the formation is subdivided into an upper dolomite unit and a lower limestone unit; elsewhere, the formation is undivided. The upper part of the formation is dominated by dolomite, and the lower part is dominated by limestone.  On the basis of conodonts and fragments of Anatolepis (the oldest known fish), the Metaline Formation ranges in age from Middle Cambrian to Middle Ordovician. The early Middle Ordovician age is based on the fossil assemblage in the upper 30 m of the formation. The uppermost Metaline Formation and the basal part of the Ledbetter Slate probably interfinger.

Chiefly gray to purple, sparsely plagioclase phyric devitrified soda-rhyolite with local glassy vitropheres, forms plug dome and adjacent sills; plug is flow-layered and contains remanent collapse blocks of pumice vitric tuff, interpreted as the White River rheoignimbrite; most of this unit is found in the Snoqualmie Pass area.

Nonbanded, homogeneous, light-colored, medium-grained gneissic biotite granodiorite with accessory sphene, allanite, zircon, and locally, garnet. Relict euhedral oscillatory zoning in cores of subidioblastic plagioclase. Potassium feldspar and quartz are interstitial. Textures mostly granoblastic, but locally blastomylonitic. Contacts with schist layers in the unit are parallel, interlayered, or locally crosscutting. Directionless, weakly foliated, dominantly tonalite; consists of hornblende, biotite, plagioclase (An25-An35), quartz, and accessory titanite, apatite, and magnetite; pyroxene rare. Epidote is common along fractures. The weak fabric in parts of the pluton probably represent an igneous flow foliation. The unit is directionless elsewhere. Ductile shear zones (a few meters wide) cut the directionless rocks in numerous places, but are less abundant than in the Reynolds Creek phase of this pluton. Divided into three units: a main tonalite phase, tonalitic orthogneiss (Reynolds Creek phase), and dioritic (mafic phase) orthogneiss. The Paleocene War Creek orthogneiss intrudes, and contains inclusions and screens of, the Reynolds Peak phase, which is about the same age as the main phase. From these relations, the batholith is given a Cretaceous age. Field relations suggest that the tonalite intrudes the dioritic gneiss and is slightly younger.

Breccia composed of crushed fragments of the granite of the Coyote Creek pluton and equigranular granodiorite of the Boot Mountain complex; present along the Omak Lake fault zone northwest of Omak Lake.

Ribbon chert in large block north of White Chuck River. Medium- to coarse-grained silicic and feldspathic gneisses and associated weakly deformed plutonic rocks. Metagabbro, metadiorite, metatonalite, silicic gneiss, fine-grained epidote amphibolite gneiss, micaceous quartzite, amphibole schist, and ultramafic rocks. Lesser amounts of phyllitic argillite, cherty phyllite, chert, graywacke, semischist, metavolcanic rocks, and marble. Rocks highly variable, commonly mylonitic and (or) cataclastic.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Mount St Helens, rocks and deposits of
