attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Medium-gray, crystal-rich, plagioclase-hypersthene-homblende dacite to andesite (SiO2 62-63.5 percent) forming steep-sided dome-shaped mass on crater floor consists of multiple lobes with rough, fragmented, scoriaceous carapaces, and flow banded, dense interiors; cracked, bread crust-like surface contains local accumulations of ash tephra and yellowish sulphur and iron hydroxide sublimates; gas and minor tephra emissions common from fumaroles on or near base of dome; dome lobes broken by smooth-walled radial cracks and thrust faults; talus blocks produced by lobe collapse fringe the dome. Average dome lavas consist of 32 percent zoned, euhedral plagioclase (An45-55), 4.5 percent prismatic hypersthene, 1.5 percent corroded reaction-rimmed hornblende, 2 percent cubes and octahedra of magnetite ilmenite, and minor corroded crystals of clinopyroxene; remaining 60 percent of rock consists of microlites of plagioclase and minor orthopyroxene and opaque minerals in glassy groundmass. Growth of dome results from both extrusion of lava and injection of magma into dome; episodic dome growth preceded by increased displacement rates of the crater floor near vent and by increase of spreading rates of the dome itself; five episodes of explosive magmatic activity destroyed portions of the dome between May 25, 1980, and January 1981. Trends in major-element chemistry, crystallinity, and mineral ratios suggest dome fed from a zoned magma chamber with initial (1980) eruption of volatile-rich crystal-poor material from top of chamber, followed by production of volatile-poor crystal-rich dome rock from deeper in the magma body.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: mostly Vashon Stade in western WA; unnamed in eastern WA
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Recessional and proglacial stratified sand, silt, clay, and gravel; thin to medium bedded; well sorted; light gray to pale yellowish brown; moderate to well rounded; matrix free; loose. Thickness commonly ranges from 2 to 50 m. These deposits are associated with three principal depositional environments (ice-contact, outwash and alluvial fan), each containing sediments with somewhat different characteristics.

Biotite-hornblende diorite and gabbro, including mafic pyroxene-bearing tonalite and quartz diorite. Color Index= 20-40. On Pratt River, mafic quartz diorite is associated with considerable amounts of thermally metamorphosed porphyritic andesite and andesite breccia.

Dark gray to black, porphyritic to aphyric pyroxene basaltic-andesite or basalt with lesser pyroxene andesite and hornblende andesite; typically blocky jointed to platy; often sheared; may contain vesicles but lack flow structures such as flow breccia; commonly resistant, forms cliffs or waterfalls in streams; locally, altered to chlorite and zeolite minerals; age generally unknown but may often be comagmatic with intruded volcanic section; small, poorly known hypabyssal intrusions; distinguished with difficulty from lava flows of similar composition unless contacts observed; easiest to observe cutting volcaniclastic or tuff units.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Crawfish Lake, heterogeneous metamorphic rocks near
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Biotite-rich schist and gneiss, calcareous quartzite, marble, amphibolite, and quartzofeldspathic gneiss, most of which has been partially or totally converted to hornfels and granofels. Orthoquartzite is a noteworthy constituent southeast of Moses Mountain and is associated at one locality with sharpstone conglomerate, a rock type common in metasedimentary assemblages of the Permian Anarchist Group. These rocks are cut by and form a series of pendants in the Swimptkin Creek pluton southeast of Crawfish Lake.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Makah Formation, middle Twin River Group, Jansen Creek Member
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Contemporaneously deformed basaltic to feldspathic sandstone and siltstone; locally encloses tabular olistostromal blocks (1-200 m long) of shallow-marine fossiliferous basaltic pebble conglomerate and sandstone; represents an ancient submarine slump deposit derived from the Vancouver Island (B.C.) shelf.

Medium-grained, foliated biotite quartz monzonite to granodiorite orthogneiss. Principal constituents are potassium feldspar, plagioclase, quartz, and biotite with minor hornblende and chlorite. Biotite-rich xenoliths of schist are common at the northwest margin of the batholith. In one area, mafic blocks, pods, and small veins mix with leucocratic material composed of quartz and plagioclase to form migmatite. Foliation, presumed to be flow-foliation due to intrusion, is oriented from north to northeast and has a shallow (25 degrees-45 degrees) dip to the west and northwest. The unit is cut by the informally named stock of Bryan Butte and stock of Sawtooth Ridge (both Eocene).

Reddish to pale-buff, medium- to coarse-grained, inequigranular, locally porphyritic syenite, monzonite, and shonkinite present as intrusive bodies and as porphyritic syenitic dikes. White and pink microperthite and orthoclase are the most abundant minerals, but the rocks contain some plagioclase. Mafic minerals generally make up from 1 to 10 percent of the rock. Accessory minerals include apatite, sphene, zircon, magnetite, and allanite. The unit generally contains 52 to 64 percent SiO2, Na2O + K2O equal to 12 percent, and no feldspathoid minerals. Granite is present locally where quartz content exceeds 10 percent. These rocks were named by Daly (1912) for exposures in British Columbia.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Big Bosom Buttes, volcanic rocks of
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Biotite dacite tuff, commonly ash-flow tuff and bedded fine-grained tuff. Also includes dacite on Middle Peak.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Dumbell Mountain plutons, quartz diorite to tonalite orthogneiss
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Greenish-gray to dark greenish-gray (CI 25-35), fine- to medium-grained, granoblastic, xenomorphic to hypidiomorphic (in massive rocks), locally mylonitic gneissic hornblende-quartz diorite; mineralogically very similar to the other plutons except that plagioclase can be as sodic as An30. Swirled foliations are common. The Dumbell Mountain plutons have been divided into three rock units. Units include hornblende tonalite orthogneiss, hornblende quartz diorite augen orthogneiss, and gneissic hornblende-quartz diorite. These units are similar chemically (i.e., low K20) and mineralogically except that the plagioclase in tonalite orthogneiss and augen orthogneiss is An38-An50 and in the gneissic quartz diorite is An30-An50. The units may represent different original plutons. The major differences between the bodies are mostly a function of deformation (the nature of the gneissic foliation; its degree of segregation, and persistence or prevalence of swirling). Contacts between the plutons and the metamorphic country rocks are varied, sharp in some places, gradational in others, but more commonly characterized by lit-par-lit interlayering of intrusives and country rock. Sheets and screens of country-rock schist and gneiss are common in the plutons, particularly between Railroad and Ice Creeks. Notably, a screen of hornblende schist and gneiss about 8 km long separates the quartz diorite augen orthogneiss from the gneissic hornblende quartz diorite. Metaplutonic rocks and orthogneisses of dominantly tonalitic to quartz dioritic composition. The rocks crop out in a belt that extends southwest from near Marblemount. This group of units includes the Marblemount Meta-Quartz Diorite, Magic Mountain gneiss, the Dumbell Mountain plutons, LeConte gneiss, and probably the orthogneiss of the Needles. The orthogneiss of the Needles and LeConte gneiss occur along strike west and northwest, respectively. This belt has been spatially and temporally related to the Cascade River unit of the Chelan Mountains terrane and appears to represent a Triassic sub-volcanic plutonic mass coeval with or closely related to a supra-volcanic arc metavolcanic and metasedimentary sequence termed the Cascade River unit. Generally, metamorphic grade in the Chelan Mountains terrane increases gradually to the southeast (parallel to the Marblemount belt) and more abruptly to the northeast from the Cascade River area, near Marblemount. The nonmigmatitic Marblemount Meta-Quartz Diorite near Marblemount is metamorphosed to the chlorite zone of the greenschist facies and is associated with medium-grade schist. Metamorphic grade increases along strike where the migmatitic Dumbell Mountain plutons and correlatives are recrystallized to the amphibolite facies and associated with high-grade schist and gneiss. The intrusive age of the Marblemount belt is Triassic (about 220 Ma) based upon several roughly concordant results of U-Pb analyses. The Magic Mountain gneiss yields discordant zircon U-Pb ages of about 195-210 Ma, suggesting that the protolith was also Triassic and part of the Marblemount belt.
Marine sandstone, siltstone, volcaniclastic sandstone, basalt, basaltic breccia, minor andesite and gabbro. Ranges in age from Late Miocene to Middle Eocene.

White to dark gray or light brown; flow banded, spherulitic and porphyritic; includes flows, domes, debris flows, breccia, and tuff; obsidian, perlite, and tuff present in some areas and are common components of debris flows. Erupted from vents in the Indian Rock area. Interstratified with olivine basalt. Maximum exposed thickness greater than 500 m.

Massive to flow-layered dacite porphyry flows containing 1-5 mm phenocrysts of plagioclase, quartz, and minor hornblende, biotite, and augite set in an aphanitic groundmass of K-feldspar, quartz, and plagioclase. Phenocrysts compose as much as 40 percent of the rocks. Plagioclase phenocrysts are chiefly andesine and labradorite. Whole-rock, major-element geochemical analyses of the porphyritic flows indicate compositions ranging from dacite to andesite. The flows are present between Riverside and Omak, near Sinlahekin Creek, Carter Mountain, Whitestone Mountain, Duffys Mountain, and Osoyoos Lake. They are generally conformable with the underlying tuff unit, but they locally fill channels cut into the tuff, and they unconformably overlie pre-Tertiary rocks in places. Thin interbeds of tuff are intercalated with the flows in places. The thickest section (approximately 600 m) of these flows is found near Carter Mountain. These flows were named the Shellrock Point Volcanics by Menzer (1982) and described as quartz keratophyres consisting of phenocrysts of quartz and pink albite in a dense, propylitically altered groundmass of glass, quartz, biotite, and calcite.  The porphyritic dacite and andesite flows are commonly strongly altered. Laumontite, albite, and/or oligoclase are secondary after plagioclase. Chlorite, calcite, epidote, magnetite/hematite, and zeolites replace mafic minerals.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Antoine Creek, hornblende tonalite gneiss of
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Medium-grained heteroblastic gneiss with prominent lineation formed by elongate crystalloblasts and aggregates of hornblende. Minor biotite strung out between partially crushed and recrystallized plagioclase. Some plagioclase has faint euhedral oscillatory zoning. Late cataclasis and chlorite-epidote alteration common.

Biotite granite. Color Index=3-7. Characterized by conspicuous quartz eyes several centimeters across which are glomerocrysts of rounded quartz grains with K-feldspar in the curved triangular interstices. Micrographic integrowths of K-feldspar and quartz common. Conspicuous chloritic alteration.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Chilliwack Group, volcanic rocks of Mount Herman
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Breccia, pillows, pillow breccia, and associated volcanic sandstone of basalt or basaltic andesite composition. Most volcanic rocks are plagioclase-phyric, some are amygdaloidal. Unit weathers orange-brown; dark- to light-green on fresh surfaces. Mostly well-bedded gray to brown and black argillite and volcanic subquartzose sandstone with minor pebble conglomerate, marble, and rare chert. Also basalt, andesite, dacite, volcanic breccia, and tuff. In sedimentary rocks, graded beds, scour structures, and load casts locally prominent; also includes some rhythmite. Locally sandstone beds strongly disrupted in argillite matrix. Rocks grade rapidly from little-deformed to phyllitic with a pronounced foliation generally subparallel to bedding. Most rocks partially recrystallized in sub-greenschist facies.

Plagioclase-quartz-hornblende-phyric and fine-grained, chloritized-silicified andesite or dacite bodies of uncertain geometry; age uncertain, but these intrusives cut Oligocene and Eocene-Oligocene rocks respectively; could have been feeders to Miocene volcanic rocks.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Snag Peak block, sandstone unit "m" of
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Thick-bedded (2-30 m), gritty, medium-grained, lithic sandstone with 5-10 m thick interbeds of thin-bedded siltstone, fine-grained sandstone, and conglomerate channel (mudflow) deposits; pebble- to boulder-size clasts in conglomerate consist of argillite, amygdaloidal basalt, dacite, bioturbated calcareous concretionary conglomerate, red and black chert, quartz diorite, silicified sandstone, rare silicified tuff, and mollusks; may in part be correlative to thick-bedded sandstone sequence in upper part of unit.

Black to dark gray-green aphyric to sparsely porphyritic, massive to vesicular basalt and basaltic-andesite lava flows and flow breccia; locally includes interbedded mafic tuff, lahar, and minor sedimentary rocks; porphyritic flows contain phenocrysts of plagioclase, olivine, and augite in intergranular to intersertal groundmass of plagioclase, clinopyroxene, magnetite, and rare brown to green glass; slightly to completely altered to zeolite or prehnite-pumpellyite facies assemblages; within contact aureole of Spirit Lake pluton, recrystallized to fine-grained hornblende- and pyroxene-hornfels facies assemblages.

Light to dark greenish-gray, medium-grained, hypidiomorphic to xenoblastic, massive to gneissic biotite-hornblende tonalite (Cl 10-35) to quartz diorite (Cl 20-40), consisting of andesine, quartz, and hornblende, and in most rocks, small amounts of biotite. Titanite, opaque minerals, apatite, and rare zircon are accessory minerals. Secondary products include small amounts of clinozoisite-epidote, chlorite, and sericite. Gneissic varieties show protomylonitic hypidiomorphic granular texture. The westernmost dike-like mass paralleling the Entiat fault is largely gneissic. This gneissic layering is dominantly defined by parallel, pencil-shaped mafic streaks and schlieren. Locally, the large mass between Hart Lake and Ice Lakes consists of layers (0.3 m thick) of gneissic quartz diorite alternating with nongneissic rock. This unit is found as irregular masses and dikes, locally as the migmatizing agent of the host rocks. The only large, mappable body is found south of Pomas Creek, which is just west of the junction of Ice Creek and the Entiat River. Otherwise, this material forms the migmatitic leucosome observed in many of the rock units of the region. The age is problematic. Leucosome formation affected Late Cretaceous plutons and predates the largely unaffected Eocene plutons. Migmatization may be diachronous across the region, the result of metamorphic, metasomatic, and igneous injection mechanisms. Units include the Entiat pluton tonalite, diorite-gabbro, and the tonalitic orthogneiss. Also includes Seven Fingered Jack pluton biotite-hornblende tonalite, and a contact complex. The Seven Fingered Jack and Entiat plutons make up a group of intrusive bodies cropping out from the vicinity of Hart Lake south-southeastward across the Holden and Lucerne areas and into the Chelan area. Seven Fingered Jack plutons contacts are mostly sharp, but locally they are faulted or gradational through a distance of a few meters. The Entiat pluton is characterized by sharp to gradational contacts or is bordered by contact complexes. The Seven Fingered Jack and Entiat plutons intrude the Triassic Dumbell Mountain plutons and are intruded by probable Eocene dikes. Several K-Ar and U-Pb ages, mostly from the Chelan area, indicate uplift in the Eocene and a crystallization age of about 75 Ma for these plutonic bodies.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Mount Rainier, plugs and dikes of
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Light-gray porphyritic andesite resembling andesite of lava flows of Mount Rainier; forms central plug and radiating dikes, and satellite plugs of olivine andesite at Echo Rock and Observation Rock; central plug altered and thoroughly opalized; age is younger than 600,000 yr.
Coarsely crystalline white marble with gray streaks. Locally associated with calc-silicate granofels and schist. Also found as small lenses in the banded gneiss, schist, and amphibolite.

Altered green andesitic breccias and massive flows and tuffs with minor arkosic to lithic sandstones and thinly interbedded minor siltstone, shale, and conglomerate. Breccias and flows contain hornblende (plagioclase phenocrysts locally present), but primary mineralogy has been largely obscured by greenschist-facies metamorphism. Metamorphic minerals include chlorite, calcite, albite, epidote, white mica, quartz, actinolite, and locally biotite. The sandstones are feldspathic to lithic. Minor pebble conglomerates, fragmental volcanic rock types, and argillites are also present. The volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks are interbedded with siltstone and shale. Geochemical analyses of metavolcanic rocks  suggest a volcanic arc setting for the North Creek Volcanics. Homoclinally northeast-dipping unit was divided into three informal members: (1) an upper member-andesitic tuff and volcanic lithic wackes; (2) a middle member-tuff breccia (flow breccia) and coarse-grained, matrix-supported breccia (lahars) in which crystal tuffs are locally abundant; these strata are interbedded with black shales; and (3) a lower member--crystal and lithic tuffs interbedded with porphyritic hornblende andesite (greenstone). The North Creek Volcanics, which crop out east of the old mining town of Gilbert, are bounded by the Twisp River Fault Zone and the North Creek fault. The age of the North Creek Volcanics is problematic. They are intruded by the Black Peak batholith (90 Ma). No fossil or radiometric age has been determined. The unit is given a Cretaceous and Jurassic age on the basis of correlations of the unit with the Methow terrane Newby Group, correlation of the unit with the Methow terrane Midnight Peak Formation (volcanic member), and its broad similarity with Cretaceous and Jurassic Methow terrane rocks.

Medium-grained hypidiomorphic-granular granodiorite and granite with subhedral to euhedral, oscillatorily zoned plagioclase in matrix of optically continuous quartz or anhedral quartz and perthite; some granopyhric textures. Color Index 10-20. Relic pyroxene in uralitic pale-green hornblende. Many rocks extensively altered to chlorite, epidote, and sphene; some crosscutting fractures filled with alteration minerals. Fine-grained mafic inclusions common. Includes some areas underlain by rocks similar to the granite of San Juan Creek. North end of pluton and smaller stocks in Monte Cristo area are more mafic and mostly granodiorite and tonalite.

Weakly to strongly foliated, light-gray to white, leucocratic, tonalitic gneiss composed of approximately 60 percent oligoclase, 30 percent quartz, less than 10 percent biotite, and accessory epidote and sphene. Foliation in the gneiss, which is defined by aligned biotite and stretched and flattened quartz, strikes northwest and dips steeply. The tonalitic and granodioritic gneiss is compositionally and texturally similar to the directionless tonalite in the Summit-Frazer complex. However, on the west side of the Summit-Frazer complex, in the Robinson Mountain area, the directionless tonalite (trondhjemite of Doe Mountain) appears to cut the tonalitic gneiss (trondhjemite of Lamb Butte; trondhjemite of Eightmile Creek). On the east side of the complex, in the Oroville area to the north, the directionless tonalite cuts mixed metamorphic and igneous rocks (gneissic trondhjemite of Tiffany Mountain). Along the eastern margin of the tonalitic and granodioritic gneiss in the Omak area, the gneiss contains abundant rafts and inclusions of amphibolitic schist, schistose metamorphic rocks, mesocratic to melanocratic gneiss, and basic plutonic rocks that form a discontinuous belt of mixed metamorphic and igneous rocks. The Summit-Frazer trondhjemitic gneiss, tonalitic and granodioritic gneiss, may be correlative with part of the Eagle complex in southern British Columbia that recently yielded numerous K-Ar ages from 95 to 100 Ma and several Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous U-Pb zircon ages. The Summit-Frazer trondhjemitic gneiss is probably correlative with the trondhjemite of Lamb Butte and the trondhjemite of Eightmile Creek on the Robinson Mountain area.
Metagabbro, biotite schist, amphibolite, and ultramafite mixed on an outcrop scale.

Medium-grained, equigranular, biotite-hornblende granodiorite that contains accessory titanite and garnet. The unit is intruded by aplite dikes and is strongly lineated; it intrudes the Covada Group along the Columbia River near the mouth of Wilmont Creek. A K-Ar age on hornblende is 71.1 +/- 2.0 Ma, but this is probably reset.

Lenses and angular blocks of sandstone, siltstone, shale, conglomerate, and volcanogenic rocks in a matrix of black shale with scaly cleavage or of intensely sheared sandstone and siltstone; includes diapiric muds, fault breccias, and submarine landslide deposits; includes part of the Hoh rock assemblage.

Limestone, dolomitic limestone, and dolomite characterized by intervals of chert beds and nodules. These rocks are light to medium gray, blue-gray, and pale yellow-tan on fresh surfaces and light gray to pale yellow-tan on weathered surfaces. Most of these rocks are fine to medium grained, but some are coarsely crystalline or aphanitic. Fossiliferous zones are found throughout the unit. Bioclastic breccias are present in some places, but most bioclastic rock is recrystallized and poorly preserved. Most rocks are fetid and contain calcite stringers and pods. Some dolomitic limestone is laminated, but bedding in this unit ranges between 0.6 m and 1 m thick. Some thicker beds are probably bioclastic zones replaced by chert; where chert beds are lacking, carbonate rock appears massive. Chert beds range from 5 cm to 8 cm thick. Chert is black, gray, and white on fresh surfaces, but because much of the chert weathers to the same colors as the carbonate rock, it is not easily distinguished on weathered surfaces.
The carbonate rocks of Limekiln Hill are assigned a Carboniferous age on the basis of conodonts and macrofossils. However, the rocks are probably no younger than Late Mississippian.

White, cream-white, and medium- to light-gray, medium- to coarse-grained, laminated to massive limestone, and dolomitic limestone, interbedded with other lithologies of the Maitlen Phyllite. The unit contains minor rounded quartz grains and muscovite. 
Light-green, green-gray, and dark-gray, fine-grained, thin-bedded to medium-laminated phyllite with thin beds and laminae of quartzite, carbonate, and sericite schist. The phyllite is composed of quartz, muscovite, plagioclase, pyrite, limonite, and chlorite, with accessory zircon, garnet, sphene, apatite, and tourmaline. The structural style of the Kootenay arc is well displayed as minor folds in the ductile rocks of the Maitlen Phyllite. 
Phyllite appears to decrease, and carbonate rocks increase westward in the Maitlen Phyllite; however, apparent changes in thickness could be the result of repetition due to structure rather than true facies changes. 
Early Cambrian Archaeocyatha (paleosponges) have been collected from the lower limestone (Reeves Limestone Member).

Thin- to thick-bedded, fine-grained, massive to thinly laminated, medium- to light-gray limestone in irregular 2- to 20-m-thick pods; contains as much as 20 percent subangular to subrounded grains of quartz, 5 to 10 percent muscovite, 5 to 10 percent carbonaceous material, and 5 to 15 percent pyrite. Calcite is stretched and forms irregular to elongate crystals; elongate pyrite lenses in limestone beds emphasize the direction of F1 and F2. The unit may in part be turbidites. Conodonts were found in limestone interbedded with the pelitic rocks.

Black siliceous and carbonaceous phyllite and argillite; gray to gray-green argillite and phyllite; and subordinate gray, calcareous argillite and light-gray quartzite. 
Argillite and phyllite contain fine- to very fine-grained (1.5-0.005 mm) quartz, carbonaceous material, muscovite, biotite, chlorite, sericite, orthoclase, plagioclase, and clay. Carbonate is rare, although argillite may be calcareous where it is interbedded with limestone; the unit locally contains as much as 25 percent carbonaceous material. Pyrite is present in places as disseminated grains; pyrrhotite and chalcopyrite are accessory minerals. Black, thin-bedded, slatey argillite locally grades into fissile black slate which contains minor beds of gray phyllite, fine- to medium-grained, thin-bedded quartzite, and gray-white limestone.
Fine-grained quartzite is medium gray and gray-green and consists of as much as 85 percent elongate quartz grains, 5 percent sericitized albite, and 9 percent orthoclase and accessory pyrite and limonite.
Bedding has been virtually erased in most places, but, where preserved, it is parallel to S(1) and S(2). F(2) folds S(1) into small closed to open kinks; where developed to a high degree, S(2) crenulation foliation essentially erases S(1) foliation.
Upper and Middle Devonian siliciclastic and carbonate rocks are exposed northwest of Metaline Falls. A limestone conglomerate with a Middle Devonian (lower Givetian) matrix and clasts containing Middle and Early Devonian fossils is in fault contact with limestone containing Late Devonian (Frasnian) stromatoporoids, bryozoa, brachiopods, and corals.
frozen water

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Cloudy Pass Pluton and associated rocks
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: White, variably fine grained to coarse grained xenomorphic or hypidiomorphic granular tonalite to granite alaskite in densely clustered dikes, sills, and irregular bodies, generally making up 80 percent or more of bedrock. Locally weakly to strongly foliated. Contacts of individual bodies are sharp. Contact of mapped concentration is gradational. Rocks rich in K-feldspar appear to be related to the batholith, but many light-colored rocks may be older associates of the metamorphic country rock

Heterogeneous complex of supracrustal schist, amphibolite, and rare marble and ultramafic rocks intruded in a lit-par-lit fashion by mostly hornblende-biotite and biotite-tonalite orthogneiss. Orthogneiss bodies range from a few centimeters thick in the banded gneisses to several kilometers thick in the orthogneiss. Abundant deformed dikes and sills of light-colored pegmatitic tonalite and lineated granite.
water

Rusty brown, thick-bedded to massive quartzite that contains 95-99 percent anhedral to subhedral, elongate, fine-grained quartz and minor sillimanite. The contact with the overlying schist is gradational; the quartzite is in sharp contact with underlying orthogneiss.
No description provided in publication

Fluvial feldspathic sandstone with subordinate interbeds of conglomerate, siltstone, and coal; plant fossils common; unmetamorphosed except where adjacent to volcanic intrusions and along strands of the Darrington-Devils Mountain fault zone.
Medium-grained hornblendebiotite tonalite; likely part of the Granite Falls stock; K/Ar age of 44.4 +/- 1.4 Ma (Yeats and Engel, 1971)
Lithic sandstone and interbedded siltstone; overlies unit Em(1c); may correlate with the sandstone of Scow Bay.
Boulder and cobble conglomerate; faintly bedded; well rounded; mostly basalt clasts; deeply weathered; overlies unit Evc.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Sandstone of Scow Bay of Armentrout (1984)
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Lithic to arkosic sandstone and minor interbedded siltstone; mostly structureless; base of unit not exposed; upper contact is angular unconformity; locally intruded by basalt dikes.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Sedimentary rocks of the Lyre Formation
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Conglomerate, sandstone, and minor siltstone in the lower half of the unit; pebbly sandstone, sandy siltstone, and minor conglomerate in upper half of unit; mostly chert clasts with fewer meta-igneous and metasedimentary clasts.
Flows and breccia; minor pillow basalt; red oxidation on some flow tops indicates partly subaerial emplacement.
Rhyolite, with minor andesite, volcanolithic sandstone, conglomerate, and breccia; locally intruded into, interbedded with, and faulted against the Chuckanut Formation.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Dacitic tuff and breccia of the Lyre Formation
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Hornblende dacite tuff and breccia; locally contains volcaniclastic deposits, rarely with leaves and wood; 46.6 +/- 0.6 Ma 39Ar/40Ar age from plagioclase in tuff; interbedded within the Lyre Formation; previously described as andesite.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Heterogenous metamorphic rocks of the Helena-Haystack melange
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Undivided rocks of the Helena-Haystack melange; includes serpentinite, metabasaltic greenstone, scattered blocks of metaplutonic rocks, meta-argillite, phyllite, metasandstone, and chert; locally contains aragonite, epidote, and actinolite; most metasedimentary rocks are moderately to strongly foliated.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Intrusive mafic and intermediate rocks of the Fidalgo Ophiolite
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Tonalite (plagiogranite) sheeted dike complex with minor layered hornblende gabbro and pyroxenite.
Serpentinized layered gabbro and pyroxenite, hornblende diorite, and quartz diorite; rare interleaved amphibole-rich layers with tonalitic layers or veins.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Meta-intrusive rocks of the Helena-Haystack melange
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Greenstone; mostly metagabbro with rare metadiorite and fine-grained quartz amphibolite gneiss; greenschist-facies metamorphism; generally unfoliated.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Metavolcanic and metasedimentary rocks of the Helena-Haystack melange
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Greenstone, metasandstone, meta-argillite, and phyllite; minor white to gray recrystallized chert; moderately to strongly foliated; difficult to distinguish from unit Jph(d).

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Metavolcanic rocks associated with the Lummi Formation
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Pillow basalt, radiolarian chert, and minor sandstone and argillite; some blueschist metamorphism; penetrative fabric
Graphitic and micaceous phyllite and minor metasandstone; strongly foliated and complexly deformed; contains lawsonite and aragonite.

Fine-grained foliated to non-foliated metabasalt; local schistosity defined by coarse-grained mica or metamorphic banding; primary textures are uncommon; metamorphic minerals are typical of the greenschist facies (predominantly chlorite and actinolite).

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Eastern melange belt of Tabor and others (1993)
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Abundant mafic volcanic rocks, chert, argillite, lithofeldspathic sandstone, and minor conglomerate and thin tuff; structurally above the western melange belt; unfoliated to weakly foliated.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Metasedimentary and metavolcanic rocks of the Trafton Sequence of Danner (1966)
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: A complex assemblage of chert, black argillite and siltstone, green tuff and greenstone, and minor carbonaceous shale, sandstone, and marble; weakly foliated.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Ultramafic rocks of the Fidalgo Ophiolite
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Serpentinized harzburgite, dunite, and gabbro; rare pods of serpentinite; locally sheared and altered to silica-carbonate rock, particularly near faults.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Ultramafic rocks of the Helena-Haystack melange
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Serpentinite and minor, partially serpentinized dunite, peridotite, and pyroxenite; widespread within the melange, even where not mapped; commonly separates blocks of different lithologies; strongly foliated to structureless.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Extrusive mafic and intermediate rocks of the Fidalgo Ophiolite
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Basaltic greenstone; locally porphyritic; locally with pillows; also contains flow breccias of keratophyre, spilite, and quartz keratophyre; local medium- to fine-grained intrusive rock of varied composition from gabbro to quartz diorite; lacks penetrative foliation; static greenschist-facies metamorphism.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Marine sedimentary rocks of the Fidalgo Ophiolite
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Sandstone and silstone, with less common argillite, conglomerate, diamictite, chert, and breccia; lacks penetrative foliation; static greenschist-facies metamorphism.

Well-bedded turbidites, sandstone, and conglomerate with local ribbon chert and pillow basalt; conglomerate and black mudstone uncommon; minor lawsonite and aragonite; penetrative cleavage or foliation.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Marine metasedimentary rocks of the Constitution Formation
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Pebble-boulder diamictite with black mudstone matrix, sandstone, chert, green tuff, and minor basalt; incipient blueschist metamorphism; penetrative fabric; similar in lithology to the Constitution Formation.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Marine metasedimentary rocks of the Lummi Formation
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Well-bedded turbidite sandstone and interbedded mudstone; minor conglomerate; shale chips and coarse grains of white and gray chert are abundant; incipient blueschist metamorphism; penetrative fabric; similar in lithology to the Lummi Formation.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Western melange belt of Tabor and others (1993)
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Marine sandstone, argillite, and subordinate (but locally abundant) chert, with rare greenstone and limestone; moderate to strong foliation (semischistose).

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Metasedimentary and metavolcanic rocks of the Goat Island area
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Foliated and bedded metasandstone, metaconglomerate, and meta-argillite; metabasaltic greenstone common; local beds of ribbon chert, diamictite, and marble.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Metasedimentary and metavolcnic rocks of the Rocky Point area
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Strongly foliated sandstone, conglomerate, and phyllitic argillite; minor basaltic greenstone, tuffaceous greenschist, and chert.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Metavolcanic rocks of the Lummi Formation
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Predominantly basaltic greenstone; minor interbeds of radiolarian chert and shale; incipient blueschist metamorphism; typically contains penetrative fabric; includes the basalt of Richardson of Brandon and others (1988).

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Alluvial and fluvial facies of the Rocks of Bulson Creek of Lovseth (1975)
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Conglomerate, sandstone, and minor siltstone; nonmarine; locally derived; only found south of the Darrington-Devils Mountain fault zone.
Siltstone, sandy siltstone, and silty, fine-grained sandstone; locally fossiliferous; structureless to poorly bedded.

Sandstone; fine to coarse; mostly structureless with some bedded sections; chert pebbles rare; unconformably overlies Lyre Formation near Woodmans and has an angular unconformity with the sandstone of Scow Bay on Indian Island.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Nearshore and marine facies of the Rocks of Bulson Creek of Lovseth (1975)
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Mostly sandstone with some siltstone, pebbly sandstone, and coal; nearshore marine environment; may either be correlative with coarse facies or may overlie it.
Tonalite and quartz diorite; U-Pb zircon ages are Devonian; likely correlates with tonalite from the structurally lower Devonian and older Turtleback Complex of Brandon and others (1988).
Diorite, quartz diorite, minor pyroxene metagabbro, and rare hornblendite; weakly to moderately foliated.
Gravel, sand, silt, and clay, in varied abundance; includes beach deposits, dunes, alluvium along river valleys, nearshore deposits, and deposits mapped as older alluvium; generally loose.

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Deposits of the Olympia nonglacial interval
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: A varied mixture of gravel, sand, silt, clay, and organic material; boulders and cobbles are rare; fluvial.
Gravel, sand, and silt, in varied abundance; placed to elevate the land or modify topography; loose to compact.
Gravel, sand, and silt; mostly fluvial; compact; locally includes silt, clay, and diamicton.
Gravel, sand, silt, clay, and till; may contain advance outwash, till, ice-contact deposits, or recessional outwash; usually compact; lacks evidence for marine deposition. Subdivided.
Clay and silt with scattered dropstones to clast-rich diamicton; lenses of sand and gravel; may contain marine fossils; may also contain advance outwash, till, or recessional outwash.

Cobble to boulder-rich silt, sand, and gravel, in varied abundance; typically loose; stratified to unstratified; predominantly composed of eskers, ablation till, and moraines; commonly has hummocky topography.
Clay, silt, and fine sand with sparse dropstones and uncommon beds of gravel; diamicton is rare; typically underlain by unit Qco or till; locally interbedded with unit Qga.
Sand and pebble to cobble gravel; local lenses of silt; loose; mostly fluvial; includes deltaic deposits and may contain small exposures of compact ice-contact deposits.
Gravel, sand, and silt; loose; may contain nearshore marine fossils; includes deltaic deposits.

Heterogeneous mixture of clay, silt, sand, and gravel in varied proportions; locally contains cobbles and boulders; diamicton and till are common; scattered dropstones are relatively common in finer-grained intervals; locally contains shell fragments.

Composite unit used where map scale, exposure, or existing stratigraphic relationships and ages do not permit separate map units. May contain small exposures of unit Qga and any of the following units: Qcp, Qc(o), Qgp(p).

Unsorted clay, silt, sand, and gravel, in varied abundance, with scattered to abundant pebbles, cobbles, and boulders; compact; typically structureless; locally contains subordinate amounts of ice-contact deposits such as eskers, ablation till, and flow till; may locally include marine deposits.
Boulders, cobbles, pebbles, sand, silt, clay, and diamicton, in varied abundance; mapped in slide bodies; unsorted; loose to compact.
Organic deposits and organic-rich sediment; typically in closed depressions.

Ash, pebbly sand with ash, and pumiceous sand; typically loose; some cobbles and pebbles of dacite and pumice; sourced from Glacier Peak; includes the Kennedy Creek and White Chuck assemblages of Beget (1981, 1982).
Dikes and sills of basalt and diabase; medium grained; dark greenish gray.
Gravel, sand, silt, clay, and organic material; till uncommon; fluvial or fluvial-deltaic; age only constrained to pre-Vashon.
Sand, silt, clay, peat, minor pebbly sand, and rare pebble gravel; contains local ash-rich layers; compact.
Mostly composed of compact, gray diamicton with rare lenses of silt, sand, and (or) cobble to boulder gravel; poorly sorted; poorly bedded; locally fossiliferous.

Sand, gravel, silt, and clay; tan to gray; loose; moderately to well sorted and rounded; good porosity and permeability; contains a mixture of dynamic-ice and stagnant-ice features, including drumlins, eskers (green lines), kettles, kames, and less-orderly hummocky topography.
Laminated to massive silt, clayey silt, and silty clay interbedded with layers of crossbedded sand; light gray to dark blue-gray; local ripple marks

attributes.DMU_100K_FULL_NAME: Pre-Vashon alpine glacial drift and nonglacial deposits
attributes.DMU_100K_DESCRIPTION: Undifferentiated alpine glacial and nonglacial deposits.
Fluvial sands and gravels and massive to laminated marine and lacustrine silt and clay; wide range of oxidation levels; contains organic material
Silt, clay, gravel, sand, and peat; coarse to fine grained; massive to laminated; predominately volcanic; abundant organic debris and pumiceous deposits.

Alluvial and lacustrine silt, sand, and gravel; compact peat beds common; weathered to clay to a depth of ~10 in.; silt is laminated and pinkish-gray; sand is gray and medium to coarse; yellowish-gray pumice common
Pumice gravel, several ash layers, and three lahars containing carbonized wood
Light-gray massive hornblende dacite porphyry and porphyritic pyroxene andesite sills and dikes; porphyry is deeply weathered in places; irregularly shaped cavities common
Irregularly shaped intrusive bodies and a sill of porphyritic andesite, probably emplaced at shallow depth
